items.title: I started a real estate brokerage at 26 and am nearing $1 billion in deals. I have no work-life balance and still knock on doors.
items.summary: Jordan Karp founded his own brokerage in his 20s and is always working — even when he's off the clock. Jordan Braun Jordan Karp launched his own brokerage at 26 and has a transaction volume of nearly $1 billion. Karp goes above and beyond for clients by ensuring around-the-clock availability. He works with celebrities and high-net-worth clients, but isn't too proud to still knock on doors. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jordan Karp, 30, founder and CEO of Jordan Karp LLC, a real estate brokerage in South Florida. Karp started his own brokerage at 26 years old and has nearly reached $1 billion in transaction volume. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I started my business at the beginning of 2023. Before, I was working on investing for my family and creating a portfolio of acquiring diverse assets from 2020 to 2022. I was cold-calling for properties to acquire, invest, assemble, buy, lease, and manage across all asset classes. I was doing it for industrial, commercial, retail, residential, single-family, development sites, creative, and opportunistic multidimensional strategic assets across Florida. I was brokering deals for myself on the side where I saw value in the market, and did that until the end of 2022. Then I started my business full-time. My transaction volume is about $500 million from January until now, and about $1 billion lifetime. I love my job because no day is the same. Here's a glimpse at what my workdays look like. I catch up with clients on restaurant rooftops, boats, and the padel court I have all different types of clients. I have celebrity clients and I also have private equity clients. I have clients who've sold businesses, CEOs, people in private businesses, founders, chairmen of businesses, lawyers, managers. One of my clients and close friends, Austin Rosen, manages Post Malone, and he has a private restaurant rooftop at the Electric Feel Studios in Miami, where I'll usually have client meetings, dinners, and spend a lot of time. I work with a lot of music artists, managers, and people in the music industry, and we'll meet at Feel. I'm very dynamic, and I'm very adaptive to where I meet clients. It's definitely important to meet people in person, whether it be at the office, on the padel court , in the street, or at a certain property. I usually work with a boat or yacht company, and they service me whenever I have a client in town to look at different properties on the water. Karp often takes clients on boats to show them properties on the water. Courtesy of Jordan Karp. If the client is not familiar with Miami or Florida as a whole, I'll take them by boat or a yacht. We'll start at the southernmost point of Miami and go all the way to Bal Harbour, the northernmost part. I'll give them a full education and information about the market, what properties trade for, the price per foot, the trends of where things are going, and they can see the level of houses. I'm available to my clients whenever they need me — even at 3 a.m. There's no difference to me between 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. — my phone is going off all day. I've taken calls at all hours of the night; I've done 2 a.m., I've done 3 a.m. When I was selling the SLS Brickell Hotel for $55 million in 2023, I was selling that for the Royal Family of Qatar, and they were based in London. I represented the seller, and I also represented the buyer, which was a private Albanian group, Kastrati Group. They were in Albania and traveling through Eastern Europe, and the main office for the Royal Family of Qatar was in London. So I was up all hours of the night. They would call me at 4 a.m., 3 a.m., and 2 a.m. They would send me documents. I'd have to get on calls with them; they were in the same time zone as each other, or slightly different ones, but a closer time zone than where I was. My work-life balance is work, work, work. My work and my life, and the balance of working within my life, are vertically integrated. I live to work. I don't work to live. For me, this is fun. It's not work. A $24 million Miami Beach, Florida, property brokered by Karp. Zoltan with Luxhunters Production Sometimes, my days run into a workout right after, and I'll take the adrenaline or the rush of work into it. I'll go on a run from where I live on North Bay Road up through to Allison Island , to La Gorce Island. Sometimes I'll run from North Bay Road down through Sunset Island, to Venetian Islands , to downtown Miami, and I'll run the properties I usually sell. I get a running perspective when I'm running by them and see, "Oh, that's an address I should keep in mind." Then I'll be taking calls for work while I'm doing that. So I'll be fielding different properties, but also fielding calls and working on the progression of that all at the same time while running those routes of the neighborhoods. Sometimes the important call comes in the middle of that time or when you're outreaching to a client, and they're busy, and the worst time for you is the best time for them. You have to take that call in that moment and bring three different people who have three different time schedules together. You're in the middle of your workout. But what you do doesn't really matter compared to what the greater goal is. Then, from the workout, I'll shower, and it'll be 10 o'clock at night, and then I'll decompress from 11 p.m. to 12 a.m. and be on my phone and still be available for calls, and look at calls that I missed while I was in the shower. I have no shame and still door-knock Door-knocking goes exactly how you could imagine. It's uncomfortable, but I think where there's discomfort, there's growth. If you come with value and you come with service and you come with persistence, I think there's a level of appreciation and acknowledgment that you went out of your way and are expensing the time to generate value and bring something to the table. People have an appreciation and acknowledgment for that, especially people on the other side, who live or have built these types of homes and have this type of net worth. They were likely, at some point, at this stage in their life, so they can relate to you in a sense; there's a connection that sometimes gets built in that way. A $51.5 million Miami Beach, Florida, property brokered by Karp. 380 Production I want to door-knock on as many homes as possible, so I'm not looking at the percentage of acceptance, but rather at the volume of business that I get from playing the numbers game. If you call 200 people and you get 10 people to respond, you're busy. One hundred ninety people are rejecting you, but the 10 people will keep you busy. And if you call 500 people and you get 20 people, you're a little bit more successful. I actually take rejection well, meaning I can handle rejection and I can continue to persist and work on that opportunity. I know there's the long term and there's a long game, and the opportunity can always be around the corner, and you just have to keep chipping away. I'm relentless, I'm fearless, and I have no shame — that's my business model. Life is very short, and at the end of the day, people want to see results. Read the original article on Business Insider

Door-knocking goes exactly how you could imagine. It's uncomfortable, but I think where there's discomfort, there's growth.

If you come with value and you come with service and you come with persistence, I think there's a level of appreciation and acknowledgment that you went out of your way and are expensing the time to generate value and bring something to the table.

People have an appreciation and acknowledgment for that, especially people on the other side, who live or have built these types of homes and have this type of net worth. They were likely, at some point, at this stage in their life, so they can relate to you in a sense; there's a connection that sometimes gets built in that way.

A $51.5 million Miami Beach, Florida, property brokered by Karp.

380 Production

I want to door-knock on as many homes as possible, so I'm not looking at the percentage of acceptance, but rather at the volume of business that I get from playing the numbers game.

If you call 200 people and you get 10 people to respond, you're busy. One hundred ninety people are rejecting you, but the 10 people will keep you busy. And if you call 500 people and you get 20 people, you're a little bit more successful.

I actually take rejection well, meaning I can handle rejection and I can continue to persist and work on that opportunity. I know there's the long term and there's a long game, and the opportunity can always be around the corner, and you just have to keep chipping away.

I'm relentless, I'm fearless, and I have no shame — that's my business model.

Life is very short, and at the end of the day, people want to see results.

items.title: The US military is preparing for mass casualties in a major war. Its dentists say it's overlooking toothaches.
items.summary: An Air Force dental assistant uses a mobile battlefield dental cleaning machine at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado., on Aug. 7, 2026. Gino Mattorano/Evans Army Community Hospital Army dentists say war games omit dental emergencies that could strain wartime casualty evacuation. Broken equipment and limited supplies can hinder field dental training opportunities. Forward dental teams can treat patients quickly and return them to duty. A painful toothache or an oral infection might not sound like an injury that could sideline a soldier in combat, but US Army dental leaders warn that in a future conflict, such easily overlooked conditions could take troops out of the fight, consume scarce evacuation capacity, and further stress a strained medical system. Most of the Army's major exercises don't include dental emergencies in their casualty scenarios, dentists said in a recent professional article , leaving commanders with an incomplete picture of the medical and triage or evacuation demands they could face in large-scale combat. Dental emergencies can quickly render troops "non-mission-capable," the authors wrote, because pain can make it difficult to eat, think clearly, or carry out important tasks like operating weapons. They described this as a significant "hidden casualty load." Unlike combat wounds, most dental problems can be easily fixed if dental teams are nearby, but despite their important role in military health care, "deployable dental capabilities continue to decline," authors wrote, underscoring an "urgent need for accurate dental emergency modeling in war-gaming to emphasize the importance of [non-battle related injuries] and dental emergencies." Past wars indicate substantial demand. Dental emergencies accounted for 19% of all treatment at military hospitals near the front lines during the war in Iraq. Another recent article by Army dentists said that dental disease and other non-battle injuries made up nearly 16% of all medical evacuations among troops fighting the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. Almost all dental patients treated by forward dental teams returned to duty after one or two visits, the authors wrote. Without dental care close to the front, however, soldiers may have to travel farther to receive treatment, potentially removing them from duty for as long as a week. Casualty evacuations for any type of health concern or injury, major or minor, are likely to pose a problem for the military in future large-scale combat. The proliferation of drones, both attack and surveillance systems, across the Ukrainian battlefield have made quick evacuation largely impossible, a stark difference from the US experience during the post-9/11 wars. In a recent military news release for a healthcare training event, Army dentist Lt. Col. Jesse Thietten said dental care "is a low-hanging-fruit solution for medical as a whole. Military medicine needs solutions to account for the anticipated systemic medical overload in [large-scale conflicts.]" Dental emergencies could rank among the top five most common reasons for casualty evacuation in such a fight, Thietten added. For troops deployed abroad in multinational settings alongside partner forces, dental concerns are "the number one reason" for casualty evacuation, he added. Thietten helped develop a lightweight expeditionary dental platform for special operations teams training in remote parts of Europe, where teams asked for help treating dental emergencies without easy access to traditionally robust medical facilities. The goal was to bring care closer to troops rather than having to shuttle them to far-off clinics. Such an approach reflects what Thietten argues the broader force will need in a future fight, including more dental work before troops deploy, along with smaller, more mobile dental teams that can operate close to units in the field. Within the Air Force, less than 1% of the service's dentists deploy," said Air Force Col. Anita Shade, chief of dental services for the 21st Medical Group, in the same news release. "Our dental teams are often disconnected from the heart of the readiness mission that we work to support, day in and day out," she said. That disconnect may become more pronounced when combat casualties can't easily be moved from the battlefield to established hospitals and care facilities. "Asymmetric/hybrid drone warfare shows us that we now need to plan and prepare for prolonged patient management in the field due to the unpredictability of patient transport," Shade said. Another problem for some military dentists is more basic — broken field equipment and a lack of medical supplies, hampering training opportunities. Two Army dentists cited those problems in another article from this summer on how military dentistry must adapt for future conflict. While preparing for a unit exercise, they found that their field equipment had not been used in nearly a year and that critical equipment including their sterilizer unit was broken, underscoring further readiness challenges. items.title: I moved away from my home country 6 years ago. When I returned, I felt like an outsider.
items.summary: The author moved from Mexico to the US and then to the UK. Courtesy of Santiago Barraza Lopez Six years ago, I left my home country, Mexico, and moved to New York, then to the UK. I recently returned to Mexico after a long time away and was surprised by how much it has changed. I felt like an outsider, and realized I had changed even more. I grew up in Mexico City and spent most of my life there. Six years ago, I left the country, first for the US and later for the UK, but I never stopped thinking of my birthplace as the place I ultimately belonged. This summer, I returned after two years away, the longest stretch I had ever gone without visiting home . I expected the trip to feel nostalgic and effortless. Instead, I was surprised by how tiring it felt and, for the first time, how slightly out of place I seemed to be. Mexico City had changed while I was away The first thing that struck me was how different the city itself felt. Mexico City had always been huge, chaotic, and international in its own way, but the version I returned to felt noticeably more cosmopolitan than the one I remembered. There were new restaurants everywhere, more international businesses , more English being spoken around me, and far more foreigners than I remembered seeing before I left. Areas that once felt deeply familiar now seemed to belong to a newer version of the city. I did not necessarily dislike any of it. But it surprised me how quickly I started feeling like someone who had missed a chapter. I was the one asking what had opened, what had closed, where people went now, and which places had become popular. For the first time, I was not the person who knew instinctively how the city worked. That was strange because I had always thought of Mexico City as something fixed in my life. I was the one who had moved away, so part of me had unconsciously expected it to remain roughly as I had left it. The city had changed, but many of the people I knew somehow hadn't Mexico City felt almost unrecognizable in places, but spending time with people I had known for years created the opposite sensation. Despite all the time that had passed, some conversations felt as though I had only been away for a few weeks. On paper, a lot had changed. Friends had gotten married, moved in with partners, started having children, changed jobs , and taken on responsibilities that did not exist when we were younger. Their lives had clearly moved forward. And yet, with certain exceptions, I sometimes found myself listening to the same stories, the same frustrations, and even the same problems I remembered from years earlier. Certain relationship dynamics had barely shifted. People worried about versions of the same things they had worried about before I left. It was a strange feeling. I had expected two years away to make everyone seem dramatically different, particularly because so many of them had crossed major life milestones in that time. Instead, I often recognized not just the people themselves, but the exact patterns I remembered. There was something comforting about that familiarity, but also something disorienting. The city around us seemed to have accelerated, while parts of the social world I had left behind felt almost preserved. That contrast eventually forced me to consider another possibility. Maybe the reason everything felt so different to me was not because everyone else had changed beyond recognition. Maybe I had. I realized the biggest change was me The last two years have probably changed me more than I understood before this trip. My relationship became more serious, and my partner and I started living together, which altered the rhythm of my everyday life in ways that felt gradual at the time but obvious once I stepped away from them. I no longer organize my days entirely around myself. We make plans together, decide how to spend our weekends, travel as a couple , share responsibilities, and build routines around one another. Even the boring parts of life, like deciding what to eat or how to spend a quiet evening, have become part of a shared structure. Being back in Mexico made me notice how attached I had become to that structure. I missed my apartment, my work routine, my evenings with my partner, and even the ordinary habits I would never normally think were worth missing. The things pulling me back were not landmarks or anything particularly British. They were simply the details of the life I had built. That realization helped explain why the trip had felt so tiring and unfamiliar. Mexico was still deeply important to me, and the people I loved there were still part of who I was, but the center of my everyday existence had shifted somewhere else. For years, I thought of myself as someone who lived in London but went home to Mexico. This trip made me realize that London is home now. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Sam Altman Now Trying to Gain Control of Electric Grid
items.summary: Armed with sordid tales of rogue AI agents escaping containment, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has found plenty of success using scare tactics to call for friendly regulation in the name of AI safety. Now, it seems Altman is riding the wave of AI fearmongering to gin up some new business partners: the electric utility executives whose companies make up the US power grid. As first reported by Politico , the CEO of the company behind ChatGPT held a series of clandestine meetings with leaders from top electric utility companies including Duke Energy, Exelon, Southern Co, and NextEra Energy , starting in July. One of the most recent discussions took place on Wednesday in Colorado, during an annual meeting hosted by the Edison Electric Institute. Dominating the agenda, Politico notes, were discussions on electrical grid security, evidently spurred by the OpenAI-Hugging Face debacle, in which rogue AI agents allegedly broke free of their research environment, accessed the internet, and hacked into another AI company. Though the incident spawned plenty of commentary around the pace of AI development and the advanced state of OpenAI’s models, the flow of information has been decidedly one-sided, with most of the details coming from OpenAI itself . As the New York Times reported , third-party safety researchers investigating the incident after the fact were only given a few days to access the reams of data generated by the hack, severely limiting their findings. That said, OpenAI has an obvious incentive to play up its own AI’s supposedly terrifying capabilities, while suppressing or ignoring evidence that contradicts its own narrative: that of rogue AI agents capable of threatening the US energy grid. To give just one example, OpenAI’s narration of the Hugging Face incident relies almost entirely on its agents’ “chains-of-thought,” where an AI model essentially generates statements explaining how it rationalized certain decisions. That sounds fine in theory, but researchers have found plenty of evidence showing that chains-of-thought aren’t reliable at narrating the actual moves made by natural language processors. Despite the unanswered question around chain-of-thought reasoning, OpenAI is using the incident to lobby for regulatory safeguards that would cement its role as the authority around AI development. This being the case, the timing of OpenAI’s energy security meetings is hard to overlook. As Politico notes in its reporting on these meetings, Altman has been hawking his company’s own cybersecurity services to top utility executives — conveniently riding the hype of the Hugging Face incident to secure a seat at one of the most important tables in the country. items.title: I fixed a tractor using John Deere’s self-repair service. Farmers aren’t sold on it.
items.summary: There is something wrong with the tractor. The water-in-fuel sensor, a small device embedded in the John Deere machine that monitors the integrity of its diesel engine, is disconnected. And I’ve got to fix it. I’m not a mechanic or a farmer. I’m poking at a laptop at John Deere’s corporate office in Santa Clara, California. There’s a cable connecting the computer to a 5130ML tractor sitting on the grass nearby. items.title: AI will transform capitalism – but how?
items.summary: Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like The idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.” The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.”

The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high.

items.title: YouTuber Markiplier's movie made over $50 million. Here's his advice for creators looking to level up.
items.summary: YouTube creator Markiplier, whose real name is Mark Fischbach. Natasha Campos/Getty Images for Mark 'Markiplier' Fischbach YouTuber Markiplier independently released a box-office hit, "Iron Lung," earlier this year. He hopes more content creators will try to take on Hollywood projects without ceding control. He said YouTubers are a "powerful entity that hold sway and a lot of eyeballs." YouTuber Markiplier thinks more creators can break into Hollywood without giving up control. The 37-year-old put it to the test earlier this year, when he wrote, directed, and starred in the film "Iron Lung." He funded the movie's low 7-figure budget himself, and it became a box-office hit that grossed over $50 million worldwide. His takeaway was that more creators should try to enter traditional media on their own, so long as they're ready to learn and wear many hats — and take on their own financial risk. "In Hollywood, it is kind of like a foregone conclusion that you'll have to give up all control to be able to do anything," the YouTuber, whose real name is Mark Fischbach, told Business Insider. "I'm like, 'No, I don't think that should be.'" A decade ago, when social media was still an emergent format, many influencers viewed a TV show deal or a movie role as a sign they'd made it. Content creators like Liza Koshy and Bretman Rock signed on to do TV shows, but YouTube success didn't always translate to TV ratings, and the results were mixed. For every web series that became a TV darling, like Comedy Central's "Broad City," there was a project that stalled out and was canceled, such as NBC's late-night show from YouTuber Lilly Singh. YouTube's gains in recent years have flipped the creator-to-TV pipeline. YouTube has become the top destination on US TV screens, reaching over 14% market share and crushing competitors like Netflix and Disney, according to Nielsen. Former TV stars like Don Lemon, Alton Brown, and Tucker Carlson are building large audiences as independent creators on YouTube and other platforms. The shift in audience to YouTube has given its top creators more power relative to Hollywood, said Fischbach, who has nearly 40 million subscribers. "YouTubers as a conglomerate are this powerful entity that hold sway and a lot of eyeballs are always on them," he said. Creators have power, but distributing a film in theaters or selling a TV show is a different skillset entirely. Fischbach thinks creators, who are used to mastering new formats and come from a DIY culture, can learn what they need to. "Learning things is the most effective way to do more," he said. "I'm playing catch-up all the time, but the more I think about it ahead of time, the more I learn beforehand, the better it'll be." That doesn't mean it's not difficult. Fischbach said even offering a digital version of "Iron Lung" on YouTube — his native platform — has come with its own set of headaches. "Even with my exclusivity deal with YouTube for distribution digitally, there's a lot that I had to learn for even setting up with their system," he said. "It's not like YouTube where you can just upload a video." Successfully pushing through the busy work and other industry red tape was part of what he wanted to prove. "I felt like it was symbolically important to carry it from start to finish" and "show that it could be done," he said. He thinks other creators can pull off the same feat if properly motivated, particularly as industry players like AMC Theaters offer new ways for independent stars like Taylor Swift to release movies in theaters. "There are a lot of creators out there that have the ability to take hold of a project and steer it correctly with their own vision," he said. "They have to expect a lot more out of themselves, and they have to do a lot more work, but at the end of the day, it'll be their vision, and it'll be something unique that only they have created." That said, Hollywood is littered with over a century of would-be movie moguls who thought they had the perfect idea, and there have been plenty of creator projects — even recently — that have failed to translate a massive social audience into another medium. For Markiplier, taking on the challenge, even with real financial risk, is part of what drives him creatively. "I really find purpose in the creative process itself," he said, noting he's not trying to step aside and hand over his business to an outside team. "My objective is not to become an empire," he added. "When I'm done, my YouTube channel will be done. It doesn't go any farther than that, mostly just because I love making things." items.title: Grandma's 72 and still working to support her children — and theirs
items.summary: Joann Ernst has played a "motherly" role in her grandchildren's lives. Roy de la Cruz for BI Joann Ernst, 72, shook her head as her older grandson decapitated an action figure. The other laid out puzzle pieces in a line, surrounded by a sea of toys. "You have to put all the Play-Doh back in the container so it doesn't dry out," Ernst called out to the 5- and 7-year olds. Ernst is not the boys' legal guardian . She's spent the past two years living with her son Jack, helping with her grandsons on weekends. Jack had struggled to work after losing an arm in an accident, so Ernst took a job in the special education department of a local school, paid his rent, and spent weekends shopping for the boys and disciplining them "as a mother would." Ernst watches on as her son, Jack, helps the boys with their technology. Roy de la Cruz for BI In June, she moved back to Oregon from Connecticut. She needed to help her daughter, Joanna, with her children in the same way she's been helping Jack and his boys. "I wish I could just be a grandmother, but I also discipline, school them, feed them, and provide a home for them," Ernst said. "I enjoy it immensely, but I'm unable to retire, and my retirement money is slowly being spent." For some grandparents, helping adult children through illness, job loss, addiction, or other crises means taking on far more than occasional babysitting. They become the family's financial and practical backstop, spending down savings, delaying retirement , or going back to work to help support both adult children and grandchildren. Business Insider wants to hear from grandparents caring for their grandchildren and older Americans caring for younger loved ones. Share your story by filling out this quick form . This year, Business Insider has spoken with more than 60 grandparents and great- grandparents raising young children or helping adult children get back on their feet, just when they thought they'd be retiring. Some have legal custody of their grandchildren. Others, like Ernst, have no official parenting roles but pay bills, provide care, and prepare them for a good life. Census data show that more than 1.1 million US grandparents 60 and older were at least part-time caregivers for their grandchildren as of 2024. The boys have been treated to many gifts by their grandmother. Roy de la Cruz for BI "Where is my Barbie?" her older grandson asks. "Barbie is long gone," Ernst replies, adding that she threw her out after her leg fell off. "She's in the city dump." "Can you buy a new Barbie?" "I'll talk about it later with your dad." Ernst raised three children, mostly as a single mother . Around 2016, her daughter Joanna developed a debilitating kidney condition that left her hospitalized for months. Ernst helped care for Joanna's children and received a small state caregiver income. "It never ceases to amaze me how, despite everything, my mom has always been there for my kids and me," Joanna, 43, says. "She always wanted to make us thrive." In 2024, Ernst moved to Connecticut to support Jack after his injury. She found a house with $1,500 monthly rent payments and began her teaching job. Now that she's returned to Oregon, she continues to pay the mortgage on her current house in Connecticut so Jack and his sons can stay there. She also works 25 hours a week as a paid caregiver for Joanna's son with autism and helps to support him financially. Ernst has supported Jack financially. Roy de la Cruz for BI Ernst has tried to balance being frugal with the instinct to give her grandchildren small treats, but even going out to the movies can become a budget decision. This isn't what she expected retirement to be. "If you look at a traditional grandparent, they get to have their grandkids for the day, take them out, and give them ice cream," Joann says. "I'm never at that point because I'm constantly disciplining and explaining things. You're never relaxed." Althea Smith, 65, has faced a more formal version of the same pressure. She is raising her grandson as his legal guardian while also providing long-term care for her own parents. Smith has a job as a full-time support worker for older adults and said she doesn't expect to fully retire soon. Ernst often would take the boys out to eat. Roy de la Cruz for BI "I want to see the world and take a cruise," she said. "I miss being able to go wherever I want. My grandson will be 18 in four years, and then I'll be able to think more about myself." Ernst's kitchen table may be filled with receipts and bills — groceries, the mortgage, and a car loan — but she says it's money well-spent. She tries to avoid thinking about her diminishing nest egg. "I know it'll all work out," Joann said, watching the boys dash across the living room. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A 43-year-old with colon cancer used AI in 3 ways to help make treatment a little easier
items.summary: Russ Read-Barrow was diagnosed with colon cancer. Russ Read-Barrow Russ Read-Barrow was diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer after seeing blood in his poop. Using Claude, he built a chemotherapy symptom tracker to help him recall what made him feel better. Read-Barrow asks AI to create a summary of his health history for new medical providers. Russ Read-Barrow has been living with incurable stage four colon cancer for five years. The 43-year-old former PR director and father of two from the UK was diagnosed with the disease in 2021. After seeing blood in his poop around six times over the course of a few weeks, he got a colonoscopy. With multiple rounds of chemotherapy and surgeries to remove cancerous cells from his colon, liver, and later his lungs, Read-Barrow's doctors have stopped the cancer from spreading further since 2022. He still needs regular chemotherapy, roughly every three months, to slow cell division and prevent further growth in his lungs and liver. "The chemo I'm having now is doing a good job of keeping it under control, but at some point that'll change and I'll have to have something else," Read-Barrow told Business Insider. Over the years, Read-Barrow has experimented with using AI to help manage the symptoms , medications, and emotional challenges that have become part of his life. In 2025, he launched a side project called FcancerwithAI, a blog where he shares his story and the AI cancer tools he's built. "I'm not saying AI is going to cure cancer. I'm saying it's going to help me remember what my consultant said, spot patterns in my side effects, and maybe give me back some control in a situation where control is basically an illusion," he wrote in a blog post . He hopes that by sharing what has helped him, he can help others, as rates of colon cancer cases in those under 50 have risen since the mid-1990s, making it the deadliest cancer in this age group. However, if spotted early, the survival rate for colon cancer is high, meaning, like Read-Barrow, more and more people are living with cancer as a chronic illness. Here are three ways Read-Barrow has used AI to manage his ongoing cancer treatment . Chemotherapy symptom tracker Russ-Barrow will need chemo for the foreseeable future. Afterwards, he typically experiences side effects like fatigue, nausea, and changes to his mood and sleep habits, which can be hard to cope with. "The hardest part day-to-day is trying to manage the energy windows I do have," he said. He started recording a 30-second voice note chronicling his symptoms each day following chemo, and wearing a WHOOP health tracker . He did this for three cycles of chemo and plugged his information into Claude to spot patterns in how he felt and what exacerbated or eased symptoms. "I found it really useful," he said. The data showed that by around day four after his treatment, he would go from feeling relatively normal to exhausted. "If you see that over time happening again and again, you can sort of deal with it better because you know it's going to come and you don't think, 'Oh God, what's happening?'" he said. Subsequently, he started asking the AI to pick out 10 things he should remember before starting his next round of chemo. One of the things it reminded him was that an anti-nausea medication he tried had helped. "You don't keep a record, you won't remember. You think you will, but give it three months and life will take over and you won't," he said. A medical history research assistant Read-Barrow uploaded all of his medical records to Gemini Notebook (formerly Notebook LM). The AI is designed to answer questions, spot trends, and create content such as presentation decks based only on files the user uploads. He uses it as a "centralized hub" for all of his medical records, which means he can access test results, doctor's notes or any other medical data within seconds. "It saves me from the massive admin headache of digging through folders every time I see a specialist," he said. Getting new people up to speed When signing up for a gym, getting a treatment such as a massage, or seeing any kind of doctor, they typically ask for your medical history. However, when you have a complex chronic illness like cancer, that history can be lengthy and painful to recount. He found a solution by asking Gemini Notebook to summarize his health history in 500 words, which he can pass on. Read-Barrow is aware that not everyone would feel comfortable sharing so much personal information with AI platforms, but for him, the benefits outweigh the risks. "I've got terminal cancer. What's the worst that can bloody happen?" he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: My listing sat for 4 months. Marketing it as a multigenerational home got 2 offers in a day.
items.summary: Scheryl W. Glanton outside the property she sold as a multi-generational home. Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton Real estate agent Scheryl W. Glanton had trouble selling a 5,100-square-foot home with seven bedrooms. She had an "aha moment" and repositioned the property as a multi-generational home . Offers arrived within 24 hours, and Glanton is awaiting closing later this month. This story is based on an interview with Scheryl W. Glanton , 74, a real estate agent from Philadelphia . It has been edited for length and clarity. It was getting frustrating. Despite at least 20 showings of my listing in suburban Philadelphia, no one made an offer. We put the 5,100-square-foot Tudor-style property, built in 1925, on the market in April 2026. I hoped it would sell relatively quickly for the $1m asking price. It was an estate sale, the area had good schools, and the neighborhood was highly sought after. Do you live in a multi-generational household? Please email Jane Ridley at jridley@businessinsider.com to share your story with Business Insider. However, whenever I asked the buyers' agents why their clients weren't interested, they said the same thing: "It's too much house." They said the seven-bedroom, five-and-a-half-bathroom home was too large for one family, regardless of whether they were planning to have more kids. I decided to market it as a multigenerational home Glanton, who has worked in real estate for seven-and-a-half years. Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton Everything else — such as its long history, a third-of-an-acre plot, stone walls, and light interior — made it a beautiful option. Four months went by, and there was no movement. Then, in August, I had what can only be described as an "aha moment." The three-story house had two distinct wings and included two sitting rooms on the second floor, two en-suite bedrooms, and a Jack-and-Jill bathroom. Scheryl W. Glanton outside the property she sold as a multi-generational home.

Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton

  • Real estate agent Scheryl W. Glanton had trouble selling a 5,100-square-foot home with seven bedrooms.
  • She had an "aha moment" and repositioned the property as a multi-generational home.
  • Offers arrived within 24 hours, and Glanton is awaiting closing later this month.

This story is based on an interview with Scheryl W. Glanton, 74, a real estate agent from Philadelphia. It has been edited for length and clarity.

It was getting frustrating. Despite at least 20 showings of my listing in suburban Philadelphia, no one made an offer.

We put the 5,100-square-foot Tudor-style property, built in 1925, on the market in April 2026. I hoped it would sell relatively quickly for the $1m asking price. It was an estate sale, the area had good schools, and the neighborhood was highly sought after.

Do you live in a multi-generational household? Please email Jane Ridley at jridley@businessinsider.com to share your story with Business Insider.

However, whenever I asked the buyers' agents why their clients weren't interested, they said the same thing: "It's too much house."

They said the seven-bedroom, five-and-a-half-bathroom home was too large for one family, regardless of whether they were planning to have more kids.

I decided to market it as a multigenerational homeGlanton, who has worked in real estate for seven-and-a-half years.

Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton

Everything else — such as its long history, a third-of-an-acre plot, stone walls, and light interior — made it a beautiful option.

Four months went by, and there was no movement. Then, in August, I had what can only be described as an "aha moment."

The three-story house had two distinct wings and included two sitting rooms on the second floor, two en-suite bedrooms, and a Jack-and-Jill bathroom. It also had two separate entrances, two staircases, and a four-car garage.

The place struck me as being perfectly set up for multi-generational living.

If I wanted a sale, I needed to lower the price to $875K and pivot.

So I repositioned the listing. This time, I marketed it toward young parents and grandparents who wanted to be under the same roof with privacy, too.

I got offers immediately

Within a day, I got two offers from multigenerational families, with one on hold in case they fell through.

The successful buyers, who are paying close to the asking price, were a couple from Los Angeles, their two children, and their aging parents from Indiana.

They'd decided to settle in Philadelphia because of a job move, a big relocation for everybody.

Glanton has spotted a trend toward multi-generational living.

Courtesy of Scheryl W. Glanton

It has nothing to do with the house, as much as the lifestyle. I always focus on that.

There is definitely a trend in the US toward three — or even four — generations living together, whether in a compound, the same house, a duplex, or a triplex.

It might be connected to affordability, but I specialize in luxury real estate. Something else is going on.

As people get older, what choices do they make about living? One of the most important concerns these days is childcare and eldercare. Multi-generational living can be the sweet spot.

There's clearly a market. As the old saying goes, it's the market that speaks.

items.title: Read the memo: PwC US is planning big changes to its offshore structure in India
items.summary: PwC is making changes to its offshore delivery center model. Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images PwC US is shaking up its offshore delivery center model in India. The US firm is planning a joint venture with PwC India, merging its offshore center with its India operation. The move will improve access to talent and technology, CEO Paul Griggs said in a memo to staff. PwC US is overhauling its offshore delivery structure in India, bringing its local operations closer to PwC India's consulting business. The US firm and PwC India plan to form a new joint venture that will merge PwC US's India-based offshoring hubs — known as Acceleration Centers, or ACs — with PwC India's consulting arm, according to an internal memo sent to staff on Saturday by the US CEO, Paul Griggs . Those hubs provide specialist talent and overnight support to US teams and operate independently of PwC India's operations. Creating a joint venture will help PwC compete more effectively as a global network, Griggs said in the memo. The tie-up would drive growth and create new opportunities, improve access to talent and capabilities, and bring the firm's "technology, engineering and AI capabilities together at greater scale," said Griggs. PwC announced the agreement early Sunday morning after Business Insider contacted the company. Neither PwC US nor PwC India responded to requests for comment. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals, the memo said. Paul Griggs, CEO of PwC US Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images Professional services firms have long used offshoring centers in lower-cost regions such as India, Argentina, and the Philippines. The hubs help firms keep client costs down, tap specialist skills, and offer round-the-clock delivery. During a consulting or auditing project, US-based employees send non-client-facing work to offshore teams in different time zones to be completed overnight. A PwC US consultant told Business Insider that they turn to PwC India when the India AC does not have enough capacity. But doing so can create delays, because the firms must renegotiate rates and terms of the work. The joint venture could speed up that process by removing "the middle man, PwC AC," they said. The joint venture also signals closer collaboration between PwC's US and Indian firms — a meaningful shift for a network built around separate national member firms. Like its fellow Big Four competitors —KPMG, Deloitte, and EY — PwC operates as a global network of legally separate firms rather than a single company. That structure is particularly important on the audit side of the business, where firms must navigate local regulations and independence requirements. "The firms that win will be the ones that stop thinking about markets, capabilities, and delivery as separate pieces," said Griggs in a press release on Sunday. The move isn't about where work gets done, but about offering clients a more seamless experience and the "best of PwC," he added. The firm is aiming to build a more globally integrated consulting model. In April, the Financial Times reported that PwC UK planned to merge its risk and consulting businesses as part of that strategy. Read the full memo sent to US staff on Saturday here: Team, Tomorrow, PwC US and PwC India will sign an agreement to establish a new joint venture that will bring together PwC US Advisory's India-based Acceleration Centers and PwC India's Consulting business. This combination will drive growth and strengthen how we serve increasingly global clients. India is one of the world's most important growth markets and a source of world-class talent and capabilities. Bringing these businesses closer together will help us connect those strengths—more effectively expanding access to talent and capabilities, bringing our technology, engineering, and AI capabilities together at greater scale, and creating new opportunities for our clients and across our businesses. Over time, the joint venture will strengthen our ability to bring more of PwC to our clients wherever those capabilities sit, support clients as they grow and operate across markets, and compete more effectively as a global network. Signing is an important milestone and the beginning of the next phase. We expect the transaction to close in the first half of calendar year 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Until then, teams will continue to serve clients and operate through existing structures and ways of working. Please keep this information confidential until the external announcement is issued on Sunday evening, Eastern Time. We're excited about what this joint venture will unlock for our clients, our people and PwC. Paul Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Anthropic Says Hackers Abused Claude to Scan 1.8 Million Android Apps for Secrets
items.summary: According to a company threat report, Anthropic states that a number of threat groups, including those motivated by financial gain and state-sponsored espionage groups associated with Russia and China, tried to misuse its Claude AI model for malicious purposes. From December 2025 through August 2026, Anthropic documented a variety of instances of AI abuse covering cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams, and other areas. Of the activities that were disrupted, one actor used Claude to create a pipeline that scanned 1.8 million Android APKs for hardcoded secrets. Anthropic has removed the accounts in question and modified its guardrails. The report also assigns the activity to the ShinyHunters group as well as to groups linked to Russia and China. How ShinyHunters Scanned 1.8 Million Android Apps for Secrets During the eight-month period, Anthropic interfered with a number of the activities associated with ShinyHunters, a group famous for carrying out large-scale data theft attacks which usually start with social engineering and the compromise of accounts. A French-speaking member who went by the handle "frkoo" deployed a credential-harvesting pipeline on ten AWS EC2 instances, the pipeline downloading the apps from various app stores and then searching the 1.8 million Android APKs for secrets. As Anthropic explained, "The pipeline mass-downloaded 1.8 million different Android APKs from multiple app-store sources, decompiled them, and used TruffleHog to search for hardcoded secrets." The confirmed findings were sent in real time to a Telegram group which was divided into more than 100 source types. An actor employed a different automated procedure to gather GitHub organization email addresses and to acquire GitHub Personal Access Tokens. According to Anthropic, it was these two pipelines that supplied the initial-access credentials that were used in most of the breaches that have been confirmed in connection with the actor. The actor also established a carding website at policenationale[.]cc which impersonated the French national police in order to sell stolen records of payment cards and the details of the cardholders. Claude Misuse by ShinyHunters and State-Linked Groups Anthropic has stated that the suspected ShinyHunters members also obtained AI API keys and used them to gain access to other organisations or carry out reconnaissance. For example, they breached a software-as-a-service provider and took the data of about 200 of its downstream customers. One of the ShinyHunters actors, with the aid of Claude, took around 34 hours to obtain more than 2,100 sets of Azure AD authentication tokens linked to over 40 corporate Microsoft tenants, Anthropic stating that "AI agents carried out nearly all of the work". Other actions carried out by ShinyHunters affiliates have included breaching a technology provider and stealing 1TB of data, compromising an airline, and gaining access to an energy company's systems. In one instance, the attacker went from a single stolen developer token to full administrative control within less than three hours. Anthropic's report also points to activity carried out by the Russian espionage group known as Midnight Blizzard, which used Claude to automate the development of malware, conduct research, acquire infrastructure, carry out phishing attacks, ensure persistence, manage command-and-control operations, and extract data. The group established a feedback loop that caused the malware to be rebuilt each time it was detected by security products. Anthropic found that the group was targeting more than 20 government, defence, diplomatic, intelligence and foreign policy organisations, employing methods such as device-code phishing, ClickFix attacks, DNS hijacking via compromised hotel Wi-Fi, takeovers of WhatsApp accounts, and malware for Windows, Android and iOS. The group carried out its operations by means of AI-powered workflows based on Claude Code skills, the human operator only modifying those skills when necessary. Anthropic has also outlined an espionage operation carried out by a group that speaks Chinese and which is known as GTG-10007, the members of which used Claude as an engineering and orchestration layer to carry out a range of tasks such as making intrusion attempts upon production systems, carrying out reconnaissance on the networks of foreign governments in the Middle East, in Europe, and in Southeast Asia, conducting vulnerability research and developing exploits against endpoint-security products, and creating malware. The group carried out automated vulnerability-research workflows while the operators were away and as a result discovered a number of previously unknown vulnerabilities in a major security product and produced working exploits for several families of network and security appliances. The operations of the group targeted about 50 organizations across a variety of sectors, including government, education, energy, healthcare, and finance, and there were confirmed breaches at an education-technology company, a retailer, and a government agency in Southeast Asia. Anthropic's Response and Security Lessons for Developers Anthropic states that it has disrupted the actors' use of Claude for harmful purposes and has therefore suspended the relevant accounts. The company also modified its guardrails in response to the misuse it had observed, introduced additional measures to enable quicker detection of future misuse, and got in touch with the authorities, industry partners, and the victims. Anthropic listed the categories of misuse it had recorded as including cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams, model distillation, and the development of biological and conventional weapons, without going into detail about the latter. For developers and organizations, the report points to several concrete exposures the attackers exploited: Check mobile apps for hardcoded secrets because the APK-scanning process specifically focuses on credentials that are embedded in Android apps. Because it can be so quickly leading to administrative control, GitHub Personal Access Tokens and other developer tokens should be carefully rotated and scoped. Since AI API keys are sensitive credentials, they should be protected, as stolen keys have been used to attack and carry out reconnaissance on other organizations. Look at the security of authentication tokens across the various cloud tenants, since Azure AD tokens are being rapidly extracted from dozens of tenants. What Remains Unconfirmed The report by Anthropic is based on the activity that it saw and stopped on its own platform, and the assignment of that activity to particular groups is Anthropic's own judgement. The full extent of the campaigns apart from Claude, and the identities of the people behind accounts such as "frkoo", have not been established. Although Anthropic states that it has banned the accounts and informed the relevant parties, it does not provide a complete breakdown of the total number of successful breaches in all the operations described. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Anthropic Says Hackers Abused Claude to Scan 1.8 Million Android Apps for Secrets appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Uber CEO Says 3,300 Layoffs Will Fund Lower Prices for Customers
items.summary: At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi stated that the approximately 3,300 corporate jobs cut by the company last week will prove beneficial to customers since the money saved will be used to lower prices. The previous week Uber announced that it was dismissing 10 per cent of its corporate staff, covering about 3,300 positions, in order to reduce the number of management layers, which represents the company's largest job cuts since the pandemic. Khosrowshahi said that the savings from the layoffs and from the insurance will be reinvested, with one of the ways being to reduce ride prices so as to encourage travellers to continue using the app. The money saved will also be used to fund Uber's autonomous taxi network. Uber's Layoff Savings Pledge and Reasons for Skepticism Khosrowshahi stated that the savings resulting from the layoffs would be reinvested in the business, specifically by reducing prices for customers. He also said that the money saved from the insurance would be put to use in lowering ride prices, a move which he thinks will cause travelers to continue using the Uber app. The company says that it intends to invest more than $1 billion in Uber's self-driving taxi service in order to compete with rivals like Waymo, and some of the cost savings will be channeled towards this initiative. Uber's performance in its most recent quarterly earnings report was better than had been expected, and Khosrowshahi admitted that the layoffs took place when the company was in a 'position of strength versus weakness'. He also said, "Some companies wait. We don't believe in waiting." The lower prices depend on Khosrowshahi's promise, and corporate assurances of this kind have not always come true. In August 2023, when T-Mobile announced it was making 5,000 job cuts, CEO Mike Sievert stated that the reorganisation would result in better value and an improved customer experience. However, less than a year later the company announced price rises for some of its older plans, including an additional $5 for each voice line every month. Uber's EU Fine and Unconfirmed Price-Cut Plans Uber has recently been hit with a fine of almost $1 billion by the EU. From 2018 to 2022, Uber automatically suspended or disabled drivers who it suspected of committing fraud or who had received bad ratings. The regulator in the Netherlands found that these decisions had not involved any human review and thus violated the GDPR rules concerning automated decisions that have significant personal or financial consequences. It has not been confirmed whether the layoffs will result in lower prices for customers, the outcome entirely depending on the CEO's stated intention. Uber has not specified the extent or timing of any price reductions, nor explained how the savings will be divided between lower prices, the investment in autonomous taxis, and other purposes. Since in previous cases similar promises have not been kept, the real effect on riders is still uncertain. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: September Windows Server Updates Break Remote Desktop Services Across 2019, 2022, and 2025
items.summary: Windows administrators have reported that the September 2026 cumulative updates are leading to failures of Remote Desktop Services (RDS) on Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025, which stops users from being able to connect and, in a number of instances, necessitates a hard reset in order to get the service working again. These issues occur after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday cumulative updates have been installed, with the servers having worked normally for a few hours before the connection failures begin. Microsoft has stated that it is aware of these reports and is carrying out an investigation. Going back to the September updates will restore the functionality but will also mean that this month's security patches are removed. Windows administrators have reported that the September 2026 cumulative updates are leading to failures of Remote Desktop Services (RDS) on Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025, which stops users from being able to connect and, in a number of instances, necessitates a hard reset in order to get the service working again.

These issues occur after the September 2026 Patch Tuesday cumulative updates have been installed, with the servers having worked normally for a few hours before the connection failures begin.

Microsoft has stated that it is aware of these reports and is carrying out an investigation. Going back to the September updates will restore the functionality but will also mean that this month's security patches are removed.

Windows Server RDS Failures and the Suspected Deadlock

As reported by the administrators, the RDS servers function normally for a few hours following the update before connection problems begin to occur; after a server has started to fail, the existing Remote Desktop sessions will not be able to disconnect or log off correctly, and new connection attempts will hang during the connection process before ultimately failing.

A number of administrators have reported that their Terminal Servers were starting to suffer the same problems. "In our environment all of the terminal servers fail (sessions drop, no new connections can be made, the only solution is to carry out a hard reset) within a day," one reader wrote.

Another stated that Remote Desktop Services functioned at first but started to fail after users had logged out: "It works at first, but after the first log out the services crash and no further users can sign in."

In that case, restarting the server made no difference, but the problems were resolved by rolling back the September update.

An administrator who was looking into the issue with Server 2022 stated that the RDP service became unresponsive when users started logging out, and mentioned that debugging had revealed what looked like a deadlock between Remote Desktop and the Local Session Manager.

The post states that the service is stuck at RDPSERVERBASE!WDLIB_Close and that no timeout has been set here, which causes a deadlock between RDP and LSM; Microsoft has not confirmed this as the cause.

Affected Windows Server Updates and the Current Workaround

The reports affect all current Windows Server releases, with administrators reporting similar problems on:

  • Server 2019 (KB5122876)
  • Server 2022 (KB5122882)
  • Server 2025 (KB5122871)

Administrators facing the RDS failures have a limited workaround while Microsoft investigates:

  1. On the servers in question, revert the September update, as the administrators say this will restore Remote Desktop functionality.
  2. When weighing the option, remember that deleting the update will also mean losing the security patches included in this month's Patch Tuesday release.
  3. Keep an eye on the affected servers since it's possible that they will carry on working for a few hours before connections start to fail.

Microsoft is aware of the reports and is investigating, with the intention of releasing guidance when it becomes available.

For now, the only method that has been reported as being able to restore Remote Desktop functionality is to roll back the September update, although this means giving up the security patches for that month.

Microsoft has not confirmed the deadlock theory nor has it given a timeline for when a resolution will take place.

items.title: A gut health scientist shared 3 recipes that help her eat 30 grams of fiber a day, from noodles to chocolate slices
items.summary: Emily Leeming is a nutrition scientist, dietitian, and former private chef. Haarala Hamilton Nutrition scientist and former chef Emily Leeming is on a mission to get people eating more fiber. Fiber helps keep cholesterol levels in check, balances blood sugar, and supports the gut microbiome. Leeming shared three high-fiber recipes that help her eat 30 grams a day. For years, fiber has had a reputation problem (boring and unsexy), but you wouldn't know it looking at Emily Leeming's go-to recipes . The former chef and nutrition scientist, who specializes in the gut microbiome , is on a mission to get people eating more fiber because it is so beneficial for our health. "Just adding seven grams of extra fiber a day is related to a significantly lower risk of heart disease, bowel cancer, and type 2 diabetes. And that's the same as about half a can of chickpeas ," Leeming told Business Insider. Beyond its reputation for aiding smooth digestion, fiber, which is found in plant foods like beans, nuts, and veggies, helps lower cholesterol levels and keep blood sugar levels balanced throughout the day. Leeming eats around 30 grams a day — a number that she said a wide body of evidence has linked to heart and gut health — but she never skimps on flavor while doing so. She shared three high-fiber, high-protein recipes from her cookbook "Fiber Power." Sesame chicken noodles Leeming's sesame noodle dish contains 10 grams of fiber. Haarala Hamilton Contains 10 grams of fiber and 51 grams of protein Serves: 4 Prep time: 20 minutes Cook time: 20 minutes Ingredients: 8 skinless, boneless chicken thigh fillets (600g) Thumb-size piece of fresh ginger, sliced 1 tbsp soy sauce 150g buckwheat noodles 1⁄2 small red cabbage, finely sliced 1 large carrot, skin on, peeled into strips 300g edamame, cooked 2 spring onions, finely sliced A large bunch of cilantro, leaves only, roughly chopped 2 tbsp sesame seeds (black or white), toasted For the creamy sesame dressing: 1 garlic clove Thumb-size piece of fresh ginger 1 tsp sesame oil 3 tbsp rice vinegar or fresh lemon juice 1 tbsp water 2 tbsp tahini 3 tbsp soy sauce Sea salt 1 tbsp honey Method: Put the chicken thighs into a saucepan with the sliced ginger and soy sauce. Add enough cold water to cover, then bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 10 to 15 minutes until cooked through. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature in the water. Cook the buckwheat noodles following the packet instructions. Drain and rinse under cold water to stop them cooking, then set aside. Blend all the ingredients for the dressing until smooth, and season with salt to taste. Add a splash more water, if needed, to loosen. Remove the chicken from the pan, discarding the broth and ginger, and roughly slice the meat. In a large bowl, combine the noodles, chicken, cabbage, carrot, edamame, spring onions, coriander, and sesame seeds. Pour over the dressing and toss until everything is well coated. Enjoy cold or at room temperature. Tuna and mango Tex-Mex salad This tuna salad contains 11 grams of fiber. Haarala Hamilton Contains 11 grams of fiber and 35 grams of protein Serves: 4 Prep time: 15 minutes Ingredients: 2 x 250g pouches of ready-cooked spelt 3 x 125g tins of tuna , drained 1 large or 2 small mangoes, diced 2 avocados, diced 4 tomatoes, diced 1 red onion, finely diced 1 garlic clove, minced 2 tbsp ground cumin 1 large bunch of coriander, leaves only 4 tbsp extra virgin olive oil juice of 2 limes sea salt and black pepper Method: Put the spelt into a large mixing bowl, breaking up any clumps with a fork or your hands. Mix in the tuna, mango, avocado, tomatoes, red onions, garlic, cumin, and cilantro. Drizzle over the olive oil and squeeze in the lime juice. Season with salt and pepper to taste, and serve. Seedy banana chocolate slice Leeming's seeded chocolate banana bars each contain eight grams of fiber. Haarala Hamilton Contains 8 grams of fiber and 8 grams of protein Makes: 12 Prep time: 15 minutes Cook time: 30 minutes Ingredients: 130g jumbo rolled oats 75g walnuts, roughly chopped 75g pumpkin seeds 75g sunflower seeds 2 tbsp ground flaxseeds 2 tbsp poppy seeds 50g dried apricots, chopped 50g dried cranberries 100g almond butter 100g honey 2 bananas, mashed 100g dark chocolate (85%), broken into pieces Method: Preheat the oven to 350°F/ 320°F fan and line a 20cm square baking tin with baking paper. In a large bowl, combine the oats, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, flaxseeds, poppy seeds, apricots, and cranberries. In a small pan over medium heat, gently stir together the almond butter and honey until loosened. You can also do this in the microwave in short bursts. Stir through the mashed bananas. Pour the warm mixture into the bowl of dry ingredients. Stir well until everything is coated and sticking together. Tip into the lined tin and press down firmly with the back of a spoon. Bake for 30 minutes until golden at the edges. Leave to cool in the tin. Melt the dark chocolate in the microwave on a low setting or in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water. Spread evenly over the slice. Leave to set before cutting into 12 squares. Read the original article on Business Insider

Haarala Hamilton

  • Fiber helps keep cholesterol levels in check, balances blood sugar, and supports the gut microbiome.
  • Leeming shared three high-fiber recipes that help her eat 30 grams a day.

For years, fiber has had a reputation problem (boring and unsexy), but you wouldn't know it looking at Emily Leeming's go-to recipes.

The former chef and nutrition scientist, who specializes in the gut microbiome, is on a mission to get people eating more fiber because it is so beneficial for our health.

Leeming eats around 30 grams a day — a number that she said a wide body of evidence has linked to heart and gut health — but she never skimps on flavor while doing so.

She shared three high-fiber, high-protein recipes from her cookbook "Fiber Power."

Sesame chicken noodlesLeeming's sesame noodle dish contains 10 grams of fiber.

Haarala Hamilton

Contains 10 grams of fiber and 51 grams of protein

Serves: 4

Prep time: 20 minutes

Cook time: 20 minutes

Ingredients:

  • 8 skinless, boneless chicken thigh fillets (600g)
  • Thumb-size piece of fresh ginger, sliced
  • 1 tbsp soy sauce
  • 150g buckwheat noodles
  • 1⁄2 small red cabbage, finely sliced
  • 1 large carrot, skin on, peeled into strips
  • 300g edamame, cooked
  • 2 spring onions, finely sliced
  • A large bunch of cilantro, leaves only, roughly chopped
  • 2 tbsp sesame seeds (black or white), toasted

For the creamy sesame dressing:

  • 1 garlic clove
  • Thumb-size piece of fresh ginger
  • 1 tsp sesame oil
  • 3 tbsp rice vinegar or fresh lemon juice
  • 1 tbsp water
  • 2 tbsp tahini
  • 3 tbsp soy sauce
  • Sea salt
  • 1 tbsp honey

Method:

  1. Put the chicken thighs into a saucepan with the sliced ginger and soy sauce. Add enough cold water to cover, then bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 10 to 15 minutes until cooked through.
  1. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature in the water.
  1. Cook the buckwheat noodles following the packet instructions. Drain and rinse under cold water to stop them cooking, then set aside.
  1. Blend all the ingredients for the dressing until smooth, and season with salt to taste. Add a splash more water, if needed, to loosen.
  1. Remove the chicken from the pan, discarding the broth and ginger, and roughly slice the meat.
  1. In a large bowl, combine the noodles, chicken, cabbage, carrot, edamame, spring onions, coriander, and sesame seeds.
  1. Pour over the dressing and toss until everything is well coated. Enjoy cold or at room temperature.
Tuna and mango Tex-Mex saladThis tuna salad contains 11 grams of fiber.

Haarala Hamilton

Contains 11 grams of fiber and 35 grams of protein

Serves: 4

Prep time: 15 minutes

Ingredients:

  • 2 x 250g pouches of ready-cooked spelt
  • 3 x 125g tins of tuna, drained
  • 1 large or 2 small mangoes, diced
  • 2 avocados, diced
  • 4 tomatoes, diced
  • 1 red onion, finely diced
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • 2 tbsp ground cumin
  • 1 large bunch of coriander, leaves only
  • 4 tbsp extra virgin olive oil
  • juice of 2 limes
  • sea salt and black pepper

Method:

  1. Put the spelt into a large mixing bowl, breaking up any clumps with a fork or your hands.
  1. Mix in the tuna, mango, avocado, tomatoes, red onions, garlic, cumin, and cilantro.
  1. Drizzle over the olive oil and squeeze in the lime juice.
  1. Season with salt and pepper to taste, and serve.
Seedy banana chocolate sliceLeeming's seeded chocolate banana bars each contain eight grams of fiber.

Haarala Hamilton

Contains 8 grams of fiber and 8 grams of protein

Makes: 12

Prep time: 15 minutes

Cook time: 30 minutes

Ingredients:

  • 130g jumbo rolled oats
  • 75g walnuts, roughly chopped
  • 75g pumpkin seeds
  • 75g sunflower seeds
  • 2 tbsp ground flaxseeds
  • 2 tbsp poppy seeds
  • 50g dried apricots, chopped
  • 50g dried cranberries
  • 100g almond butter
  • 100g honey
  • 2 bananas, mashed
  • 100g dark chocolate (85%), broken into pieces

Method:

  1. Preheat the oven to 350°F/ 320°F fan and line a 20cm square baking tin with baking paper.
  1. In a large bowl, combine the oats, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, flaxseeds, poppy seeds, apricots, and cranberries.
  1. In a small pan over medium heat, gently stir together the almond butter and honey until loosened. You can also do this in the microwave in short bursts. Stir through the mashed bananas.
  1. Pour the warm mixture into the bowl of dry ingredients. Stir well until everything is coated and sticking together.
  1. Tip into the lined tin and press down firmly with the back of a spoon. Bake for 30 minutes until golden at the edges.
  1. Leave to cool in the tin.
  1. Melt the dark chocolate in the microwave on a low setting or in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water. Spread evenly over the slice.
  1. Leave to set before cutting into 12 squares.

items.title: Blizzard Announces StarCraft Returns in 2030 as an Open-World Shooter
items.summary: Blizzard Entertainment announced the return of StarCraft with a new open-world shooter which will be released in 2030 during the Opening Ceremony of BlizzCon 2026. This is the series' first new game in nearly ten years and represents a move away from the strategy games which established StarCraft as a well-known name. The game is titled StarCraft and is being headed by Dan Hay, former executive producer of Far Cry. Beyond a first trailer there are few details, the release being framed by an open-world shooter. "Here we are finally making StarCraft," Hay said on stage. Blizzard's New StarCraft Shooter, Past Attempts, and 2030 Release The statement confirmed that the game is titled StarCraft, that it is an open-world shooter, and that Dan Hay is in charge of it having previously been the executive producer on Far Cry; additionally, Blizzard presented a debut cinematic trailer to set the tone. Apart from that, no further information is available. StarCraft (2030) is the first game in the series after StarCraft Remastered in 2017 and the first entirely new entry since the single-player DLC StarCraft: Nova Covert Ops in 2016. Blizzard has not been the first time it has tried to adapt its strategy series into a shooter; the StarCraft: Ghost project was indeed being developed decades ago for the PS2, the original Xbox, and the GameCube as a stealth-shooter, but it was eventually quietly canceled. The more up-to-date reports suggest that Nexon could be developing another game in the series, even though this new StarCraft seems to be unrelated. The 2030 version of StarCraft is aiming for a 2030 launch. Blizzard has not specified a particular date, platforms, or provided any gameplay details other than the description of an open-world shooter and the announcement trailer. The company states that further information will be posted on the official StarCraft website over time. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Blizzard Announces StarCraft Returns in 2030 as an Open-World Shooter appeared first on gHacks .
