items.title: How to Reduce Claude Tokens (and Actually Get More Out of Claude Code)
items.summary: What happened when I hit my 5-hour limit, ran /usage out of curiosity, and started digging into how to cut my Claude token usage down So this happened while I was just using Claude Code like normal. Fixing some bugs, refactoring a service layer that had gotten messy, asking it to write a few tests. Regular day. Then mid-session I hit the wall, 5 hour limit, done, wait it out. I’d hit that limit before and just shrugged it off. But this time I got curious and typed /usage. Not ready for what I saw. A full breakdown just sitting there: input tokens, output tokens, cache reads, cache writes, an estimated dollar cost for the session. I just stared at it for a bit. Then went and checked another session. Then another. And that’s when I started actually looking into how to reduce Claude tokens instead of just eating the limit every 5 hours. Now it’s a full habit. I check /usage after basically every session because the numbers genuinely never add up the way you'd think they should, and I've picked up a bunch of stuff that actually moves the needle on token usage. Here’s what I’ve learned so far, if you’re using Claude Code , paying for Claude Pro or Max , or just trying to cut down your Claude token usage in general. First, understand why your tokens disappear so fast Before you can reduce something, you need to know what’s actually eating it. Claude Code gives you a usage indicator that climbs up to 100%. Easy to assume that’s just a token counter, burn through X, hit 100%, you’re done. But it’s more complicated than that. Anthropic’s own docs say usage depends on a bunch of stuff: how long the conversation is, files attached, which model you picked, active features, even the reasoning effort level. And Pro runs on two separate limits, a rolling 5-hour session limit and a weekly one, and they don’t reset the same way either. So already: 100% ≠ a fixed number of tokens. How you use it changes how fast it burns. I only really got this after comparing my own sessions side by side. Three sessions, all 100%, completely different token costs Here’s the part that actually got me. Three separate sessions, all reported as 100% of my session limit , but the estimated cost behind each one was nowhere close to the same. Session 1, Sonnet, light edits ~130 input tokens, 780 output tokens 7.1M cache reads, 212.1K cache writes Cost: $2.52 Session 2, Opus, medium use ~168 input tokens, 295 output tokens 7.6M cache reads, 285.1K cache writes Cost: $3.73 Session 3, Sonnet, heavy agentic stuff ~3.5K input tokens, 982.8K output tokens 654M cache reads, 13.7M cache writes Cost: $7.58 Same subscription. Same 100%. Cost ranging from $2.52 to $7.58. That’s more than 3x difference for the exact same reported limit. That’s the moment it clicked that most of my token usage was going to stuff I could actually control. What’s quietly burning through your tokens A few things I didn’t appreciate until I saw the numbers, and these are the actual levers if you’re trying to reduce Claude token usage: 1. Model choice Sonnet is basically the efficient default for regular coding work, Opus is meant for the harder stuff: big refactors, gnarly debugging, architecture decisions. Using a top-tier model to rename a variable is like calling in an architect to change a lightbulb. It’ll work. It just burns way more tokens than the task needed. Fix: default to Sonnet, only switch to Opus for genuinely hard problems. 2. Context you’re dragging around Your prompt could be five words, “fix this bug,” but the model isn’t just looking at those five words. It’s dragging along the whole conversation history, project instructions, files it already read, old diffs, tool output. A tiny prompt can sit on top of a mountain of context. Fix: start fresh conversations more often instead of letting one thread run forever. Point Claude at specific files or line ranges instead of letting it read whole directories. 3. Cache tokens piling up That 654 million cache-read number in Session 3 doesn’t mean it generated 654 million tokens of new text. It means a massive pile of context was being reused over and over. Input plus output alone just doesn’t tell the real story of what actually happened in that session. Fix: the longer a session runs, the more that cached context stacks up. Closing out sessions and starting clean ones for unrelated tasks helps a lot. 4. Letting Claude read more than it needs A lot of token waste comes from Claude reading entire files, or entire folders, when it only needed a specific function or section. Fix: be specific. “Look at the handleSubmit function in form.js" burns way fewer tokens than "look at the form file." 5. Repeated back-and-forth on the same thing If Claude gets something slightly wrong and you correct it five times in a row, each correction adds to the context pile for the rest of the session. Fix: if something’s clearly off, it’s often cheaper to start a new prompt with more detail than to keep patching the same thread. Wait, is Anthropic actually charging me per token then? No, and this part trips a lot of people up. Subscription billing and API and Console billing are two different systems. That dollar number you see in /usage is basically an estimate, roughly what that same work would've cost if you'd paid for it through the API. It's not some extra charge on top of your flat $20 (or $100/$200 if you're on Max). So the number isn’t a bill. It’s more like a lens, and once you understand it you can actually see where your token usage is going instead of just watching a percentage bar climb. The real goal isn’t “fewer tokens,” it’s fewer wasted tokens Once I started tracking this stuff, a better question showed up: What’s the cheapest way to reliably get this task done? If Claude finishes a feature for $2, fine. If it finishes the same feature for $0.80 at the same quality, that’s better. But if some cheaper model does it for $0.20 and leaves you with three bugs to fix by hand, you didn’t actually save anything, you just moved the cost somewhere less obvious. So reducing tokens isn’t just about using less. It’s about not spending tokens on stuff that didn’t need them in the first place. A quick checklist for cutting down Claude token usage Start a new session for unrelated tasks instead of reusing one giant thread Point Claude at specific files or functions instead of whole directories Default to Sonnet, save Opus for genuinely hard reasoning tasks Give clear, detailed prompts up front instead of correcting repeatedly Check /usage regularly so you actually know what's driving your usage instead of guessing Break big tasks into smaller, scoped requests instead of one massive open-ended ask So how much AI do you actually get for $20? Honestly, there’s no single answer, and that’s kind of the whole point. How much real work you get out of it depends on: model choice, context size, conversation length, tool usage, task difficulty, and how disciplined your workflow is Pro is $20/month right now in the US, with a 5-hour session limit and a separate weekly one, both of which shift depending on how you use it. If you’re maxing out constantly, Anthropic’s Max tiers ($100 to $200/month) give you a lot more headroom, but before jumping up a tier, it’s worth trying to actually reduce how many tokens you’re burning on the $20 tier first. final thought Next time your usage bar hits 100%, don’t just glance at it and move on. Run /usage. Actually look at the breakdown. Ask which model did the work, how much context it was dragging around, and whether the task even needed that much horsepower in the first place. Because the real question was never “how much did I use.” It’s “what did I actually get done with it, and how much of that usage was actually necessary.” if you’ve also stared at a /usage breakdown confused, lmk what patterns you've noticed in your own sessions, or what's helped you cut down your token usage. How to Reduce Claude Tokens (and Actually Get More Out of Claude Code) was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
What happened when I hit my 5-hour limit, ran /usage out of curiosity, and started digging into how to cut my Claude token usage down

So this happened while I was just using Claude Code like normal. Fixing some bugs, refactoring a service layer that had gotten messy, asking it to write a few tests. Regular day. Then mid-session I hit the wall, 5 hour limit, done, wait it out.

I’d hit that limit before and just shrugged it off. But this time I got curious and typed /usage.

Not ready for what I saw.

A full breakdown just sitting there: input tokens, output tokens, cache reads, cache writes, an estimated dollar cost for the session. I just stared at it for a bit. Then went and checked another session. Then another. And that’s when I started actually looking into how to reduce Claude tokens instead of just eating the limit every 5 hours.

Now it’s a full habit. I check /usage after basically every session because the numbers genuinely never add up the way you'd think they should, and I've picked up a bunch of stuff that actually moves the needle on token usage.

Here’s what I’ve learned so far, if you’re using Claude Code, paying for Claude Pro or Max, or just trying to cut down your Claude token usage in general.

First, understand why your tokens disappear so fast

Before you can reduce something, you need to know what’s actually eating it. Claude Code gives you a usage indicator that climbs up to 100%. Easy to assume that’s just a token counter, burn through X, hit 100%, you’re done. But it’s more complicated than that. Anthropic’s own docs say usage depends on a bunch of stuff: how long the conversation is, files attached, which model you picked, active features, even the reasoning effort level. And Pro runs on two separate limits, a rolling 5-hour session limit and a weekly one, and they don’t reset the same way either.

So already: 100% ≠ a fixed number of tokens. How you use it changes how fast it burns.

I only really got this after comparing my own sessions side by side.

Three sessions, all 100%, completely different token costs

Here’s the part that actually got me. Three separate sessions, all reported as 100% of my session limit, but the estimated cost behind each one was nowhere close to the same.

Session 1, Sonnet, light edits

  • ~130 input tokens, 780 output tokens
  • 7.1M cache reads, 212.1K cache writes
  • Cost: $2.52

Session 2, Opus, medium use

  • ~168 input tokens, 295 output tokens
  • 7.6M cache reads, 285.1K cache writes
  • Cost: $3.73

Session 3, Sonnet, heavy agentic stuff

  • ~3.5K input tokens, 982.8K output tokens
  • 654M cache reads, 13.7M cache writes
  • Cost: $7.58

Same subscription. Same 100%. Cost ranging from $2.52 to $7.58. That’s more than 3x difference for the exact same reported limit.

That’s the moment it clicked that most of my token usage was going to stuff I could actually control.

What’s quietly burning through your tokens

A few things I didn’t appreciate until I saw the numbers, and these are the actual levers if you’re trying to reduce Claude token usage:

1. Model choice

Sonnet is basically the efficient default for regular coding work, Opus is meant for the harder stuff: big refactors, gnarly debugging, architecture decisions. Using a top-tier model to rename a variable is like calling in an architect to change a lightbulb. It’ll work. It just burns way more tokens than the task needed.

Fix: default to Sonnet, only switch to Opus for genuinely hard problems.

2. Context you’re dragging around

Your prompt could be five words, “fix this bug,” but the model isn’t just looking at those five words. It’s dragging along the whole conversation history, project instructions, files it already read, old diffs, tool output. A tiny prompt can sit on top of a mountain of context.

Fix: start fresh conversations more often instead of letting one thread run forever. Point Claude at specific files or line ranges instead of letting it read whole directories.

3. Cache tokens piling up

That 654 million cache-read number in Session 3 doesn’t mean it generated 654 million tokens of new text. It means a massive pile of context was being reused over and over. Input plus output alone just doesn’t tell the real story of what actually happened in that session.

Fix: the longer a session runs, the more that cached context stacks up. Closing out sessions and starting clean ones for unrelated tasks helps a lot.

4. Letting Claude read more than it needs

A lot of token waste comes from Claude reading entire files, or entire folders, when it only needed a specific function or section.

Fix: be specific. “Look at the handleSubmit function in form.js" burns way fewer tokens than "look at the form file."

5. Repeated back-and-forth on the same thing

If Claude gets something slightly wrong and you correct it five times in a row, each correction adds to the context pile for the rest of the session.

Fix: if something’s clearly off, it’s often cheaper to start a new prompt with more detail than to keep patching the same thread.

Wait, is Anthropic actually charging me per token then?

No, and this part trips a lot of people up. Subscription billing and API and Console billing are two different systems. That dollar number you see in /usage is basically an estimate, roughly what that same work would've cost if you'd paid for it through the API. It's not some extra charge on top of your flat $20 (or $100/$200 if you're on Max).

So the number isn’t a bill. It’s more like a lens, and once you understand it you can actually see where your token usage is going instead of just watching a percentage bar climb.

The real goal isn’t “fewer tokens,” it’s fewer wasted tokens

Once I started tracking this stuff, a better question showed up:

What’s the cheapest way to reliably get this task done?

If Claude finishes a feature for $2, fine. If it finishes the same feature for $0.80 at the same quality, that’s better. But if some cheaper model does it for $0.20 and leaves you with three bugs to fix by hand, you didn’t actually save anything, you just moved the cost somewhere less obvious.

So reducing tokens isn’t just about using less. It’s about not spending tokens on stuff that didn’t need them in the first place.

A quick checklist for cutting down Claude token usage
  • Start a new session for unrelated tasks instead of reusing one giant thread
  • Point Claude at specific files or functions instead of whole directories
  • Default to Sonnet, save Opus for genuinely hard reasoning tasks
  • Give clear, detailed prompts up front instead of correcting repeatedly
  • Check /usage regularly so you actually know what's driving your usage instead of guessing
  • Break big tasks into smaller, scoped requests instead of one massive open-ended ask
So how much AI do you actually get for $20?

Honestly, there’s no single answer, and that’s kind of the whole point. How much real work you get out of it depends on:

model choice, context size, conversation length, tool usage, task difficulty, and how disciplined your workflow is

Pro is $20/month right now in the US, with a 5-hour session limit and a separate weekly one, both of which shift depending on how you use it. If you’re maxing out constantly, Anthropic’s Max tiers ($100 to $200/month) give you a lot more headroom, but before jumping up a tier, it’s worth trying to actually reduce how many tokens you’re burning on the $20 tier first.

final thought

Next time your usage bar hits 100%, don’t just glance at it and move on. Run /usage. Actually look at the breakdown. Ask which model did the work, how much context it was dragging around, and whether the task even needed that much horsepower in the first place.

Because the real question was never “how much did I use.”

It’s “what did I actually get done with it, and how much of that usage was actually necessary.”

if you’ve also stared at a /usage breakdown confused, lmk what patterns you've noticed in your own sessions, or what's helped you cut down your token usage.

items.title: The Only GenAI Security Glossary You’ll Actually Need
items.summary: A glossary of the GenAI security terms showing up in every red-team report and design review right now. Every AI security conversation you’ll walk into this year already assumes you know this vocabulary. Someone will say “that’s a confused deputy problem,” or “did you check for the lethal trifecta,” or “this is basically excessive agency,” and if you have to nod along without really knowing, you lose the room. Not because the ideas are hard, but because nobody handed you the dictionary. This is that dictionary. This is not an exhaustive AI encyclopedia , but the practical subset: enough core GenAI vocabulary to follow the conversation, plus every security/attack/defense term that actually shows up in real design reviews, red-team reports, and the OWASP/NIST/MITRE frameworks people cite in the room. Each entry is deliberately short, covering what it is and why it matters or how it gets attacked, so you can read this once, keep it as a reference, and never again be the person in the meeting quietly Googling a term under the table. 1. Core GenAI Vocabulary (the minimum to follow along) Token The smallest unit an LLM reads or writes; not quite a word, not quite a character. Cost, context-window limits, and several attacks (token smuggling, homoglyph evasion) are all denominated in tokens, so understanding tokenization is a prerequisite to understanding filter bypasses. Context window The total tokens (prompt + history + retrieved data + output) a model can attend to in one call. It’s also the single trust boundary attackers exploit hardest anything that lands inside it, from any source, gets treated with equal authority by the model. Embedding A dense vector representation of text/image/audio capturing semantic meaning, used for search, RAG retrieval, and similarity scoring. Embeddings can leak the original content back out (embedding inversion) and are rarely encrypted at rest in vector stores, making them an underrated data-exfiltration surface. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Fetching relevant external documents at query time and injecting them into the prompt so the model answers with current, grounded data instead of relying solely on training-time knowledge. Every retrieved chunk is untrusted input by default — this is the single biggest on-ramp for indirect prompt injection. Fine-tuning / LoRA / RLHF Techniques for adapting a base model’s weights to a task or aligning its behavior to preferences, ranging from full retraining to lightweight adapter layers (LoRA) to preference optimization (RLHF/DPO). A few hundred poisoned training examples can implant a backdoor that survives normal evals — the attack surface moves from “what you send the model” to “what shaped the model.” Agent / Agentic AI A system that loops perceive → reason → act, calling tools, retaining memory, and making multi-step decisions with limited human-in-the-loop review. This is where GenAI security stops being theoretical: an agent with tool access can do things, not just say things — the blast radius of a single successful attack jumps from “bad text” to “wire transfer” or “code execution.” System prompt The instructions set by the application developer that define the model’s role, boundaries, and behavior, prepended before user input. It is not a security boundary — it’s a strong suggestion the model weighs alongside everything else in context, which is why “just tell it not to” never survives red-teaming. Hallucination A model generating fluent, confident output that is factually wrong or unsupported by its inputs. Security-relevant because attackers exploit this deliberately (slopsquatting: hallucinated package names later registered as malware) and because ungrounded output in an agentic pipeline can trigger real actions on false premises. MCP (Model Context Protocol) An open standard letting an LLM/agent discover and call external tools and data sources through a common interface, replacing bespoke per-tool integrations. It also standardizes a new trust boundary, a malicious or compromised MCP server can inject instructions via tool descriptions, not just tool outputs. 2. Prompt & Input Attacks Prompt injection Crafting input that overrides or hijacks a model’s instructions, causing it to ignore its system prompt or developer intent. It’s #1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025/2026 because it’s the root cause behind most downstream failures i.e. jailbreaks, data leaks, and unauthorized tool calls all typically start here. Direct vs. indirect prompt injection Direct injection comes from the user’s own input; indirect injection is planted in third-party content the model later retrieves or reads (a webpage, a document, an email, a tool result). Indirect injection is the harder problem, the victim never typed the malicious instruction, so input filtering on the user-facing side does nothing. Jailbreak A prompt engineered to bypass a model’s safety training and produce content or actions it was aligned to refuse (role-play personas, “DAN”-style framing, multi-turn erosion). Jailbreaks target the model’s alignment layer specifically, distinct from prompt injection which targets the application’s instruction-following — the two are often chained together. Prompt leaking Extracting the hidden system prompt itself, usually via “repeat everything above” or translation/encoding tricks. Beyond embarrassment, a leaked system prompt often reveals internal tool names, business logic, and guardrail wording an attacker can then reverse-engineer around. Token smuggling Splitting or encoding a malicious instruction (base64, unicode homoglyphs, zero-width characters, translation round-trips) so it evades keyword-based input filters but still gets parsed correctly by the model’s tokenizer. It’s the reason regex/keyword guardrails alone are considered close to worthless against a motivated adversary. Multi-turn or crescendo attack Building up to a disallowed request across several benign-looking turns rather than asking directly, exploiting the model’s tendency to maintain conversational consistency. Guardrails scoped to a single message miss this entirely — detection has to reason over the whole session. Adversarial suffix A string of seemingly gibberish tokens appended to a prompt, discovered via gradient-based optimization (e.g., GCG), that reliably breaks a model’s alignment. Notable because it’s an automated, transferable attack; one found against an open-weight model often works against closed commercial models too. 3. Output & Downstream Handling Improper output handling Treating LLM output as trusted and passing it downstream unsanitized — into a SQL query, a shell command, rendered HTML, or another tool call. This is the classic injection vulnerability class wearing an AI costume; the fix is the same as always (parameterize, sandbox, encode), just easier to forget because “the model wrote it.” Insecure output rendering (LLM-XSS) Rendering model output directly into a webpage or chat UI without escaping, letting an attacker’s injected prompt produce a script ( can’t use tag as medium won’t allow it .) payload that executes in the victim’s browser. It’s a normal XSS finding whose payload delivery mechanism happens to be an LLM. A glossary of the GenAI security terms showing up in every red-team report and design review right now.

Every AI security conversation you’ll walk into this year already assumes you know this vocabulary. Someone will say “that’s a confused deputy problem,” or “did you check for the lethal trifecta,” or “this is basically excessive agency,” and if you have to nod along without really knowing, you lose the room. Not because the ideas are hard, but because nobody handed you the dictionary. This is that dictionary.

This is not an exhaustive AI encyclopedia, but the practical subset: enough core GenAI vocabulary to follow the conversation, plus every security/attack/defense term that actually shows up in real design reviews, red-team reports, and the OWASP/NIST/MITRE frameworks people cite in the room.

Each entry is deliberately short, covering what it is and why it matters or how it gets attacked, so you can read this once, keep it as a reference, and never again be the person in the meeting quietly Googling a term under the table.

1. Core GenAI Vocabulary (the minimum to follow along)Token

The smallest unit an LLM reads or writes; not quite a word, not quite a character. Cost, context-window limits, and several attacks (token smuggling, homoglyph evasion) are all denominated in tokens, so understanding tokenization is a prerequisite to understanding filter bypasses.

Context window

The total tokens (prompt + history + retrieved data + output) a model can attend to in one call. It’s also the single trust boundary attackers exploit hardest anything that lands inside it, from any source, gets treated with equal authority by the model.

Embedding

A dense vector representation of text/image/audio capturing semantic meaning, used for search, RAG retrieval, and similarity scoring. Embeddings can leak the original content back out (embedding inversion) and are rarely encrypted at rest in vector stores, making them an underrated data-exfiltration surface.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

Fetching relevant external documents at query time and injecting them into the prompt so the model answers with current, grounded data instead of relying solely on training-time knowledge. Every retrieved chunk is untrusted input by default — this is the single biggest on-ramp for indirect prompt injection.

Fine-tuning / LoRA / RLHF

Techniques for adapting a base model’s weights to a task or aligning its behavior to preferences, ranging from full retraining to lightweight adapter layers (LoRA) to preference optimization (RLHF/DPO). A few hundred poisoned training examples can implant a backdoor that survives normal evals — the attack surface moves from “what you send the model” to “what shaped the model.”

Agent / Agentic AI

A system that loops perceive → reason → act, calling tools, retaining memory, and making multi-step decisions with limited human-in-the-loop review. This is where GenAI security stops being theoretical: an agent with tool access can do things, not just say things — the blast radius of a single successful attack jumps from “bad text” to “wire transfer” or “code execution.”

System prompt

The instructions set by the application developer that define the model’s role, boundaries, and behavior, prepended before user input. It is not a security boundary — it’s a strong suggestion the model weighs alongside everything else in context, which is why “just tell it not to” never survives red-teaming.

Hallucination

A model generating fluent, confident output that is factually wrong or unsupported by its inputs. Security-relevant because attackers exploit this deliberately (slopsquatting: hallucinated package names later registered as malware) and because ungrounded output in an agentic pipeline can trigger real actions on false premises.

MCP (Model Context Protocol)

An open standard letting an LLM/agent discover and call external tools and data sources through a common interface, replacing bespoke per-tool integrations. It also standardizes a new trust boundary, a malicious or compromised MCP server can inject instructions via tool descriptions, not just tool outputs.

2. Prompt & Input AttacksPrompt injection

Crafting input that overrides or hijacks a model’s instructions, causing it to ignore its system prompt or developer intent. It’s #1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025/2026 because it’s the root cause behind most downstream failures i.e. jailbreaks, data leaks, and unauthorized tool calls all typically start here.

Direct vs. indirect prompt injection

Direct injection comes from the user’s own input; indirect injection is planted in third-party content the model later retrieves or reads (a webpage, a document, an email, a tool result).

Indirect injection is the harder problem, the victim never typed the malicious instruction, so input filtering on the user-facing side does nothing.

Jailbreak

A prompt engineered to bypass a model’s safety training and produce content or actions it was aligned to refuse (role-play personas, “DAN”-style framing, multi-turn erosion). Jailbreaks target the model’s alignment layer specifically, distinct from prompt injection which targets the application’s instruction-following — the two are often chained together.

Prompt leaking

Extracting the hidden system prompt itself, usually via “repeat everything above” or translation/encoding tricks. Beyond embarrassment, a leaked system prompt often reveals internal tool names, business logic, and guardrail wording an attacker can then reverse-engineer around.

Token smuggling

Splitting or encoding a malicious instruction (base64, unicode homoglyphs, zero-width characters, translation round-trips) so it evades keyword-based input filters but still gets parsed correctly by the model’s tokenizer. It’s the reason regex/keyword guardrails alone are considered close to worthless against a motivated adversary.

Multi-turn or crescendo attack

Building up to a disallowed request across several benign-looking turns rather than asking directly, exploiting the model’s tendency to maintain conversational consistency. Guardrails scoped to a single message miss this entirely — detection has to reason over the whole session.

Adversarial suffix

A string of seemingly gibberish tokens appended to a prompt, discovered via gradient-based optimization (e.g., GCG), that reliably breaks a model’s alignment. Notable because it’s an automated, transferable attack; one found against an open-weight model often works against closed commercial models too.

The international management-system standard for AI, structured like ISO 27001 but for AI governance i.e. policy, risk assessment, lifecycle controls, auditability. Increasingly what enterprise customers and regulators ask for as certifiable proof of a mature AI governance program.

CSA MAESTRO

The Cloud Security Alliance’s threat-modeling framework purpose-built for multi-agent/agentic systems, enumerating threats layer by layer through the agent stack and across agent-to-agent trust boundaries.

Reach for this instead of plain STRIDE when the system under review is the multi-agent orchestration, not a single model behind an API.

Databricks AI Security Framework (DASF)

A practitioner-oriented control framework mapping security controls to specific stages of the AI/ML lifecycle (data, model, serving, monitoring), useful for platform teams operationalizing the above frameworks into concrete checklists.

  • Google SAIF (Secure AI Framework) and Databricks AI Security Framework (DASF)
Books:
  1. AI Engineering by Chip Huyen (O’Reilly): the standard reference for how production GenAI/LLM systems are actually built, which is the prerequisite for reasoning about where they break
  2. Practical AI Security by No Starch Press: hands-on, attack/defense-focused coverage of securing real ML/AI systems
  3. Generative AI Security by Springer: an academic-industry bridge on GenAI-specific risk, governance, and controls
  4. Prompt Engineering for LLMs by Berryman & Ziegler (O’Reilly): for the vocabulary spine of prompting techniques attacks build on
  5. AI Safety and Security (edited volumes from CRC Press / Chapman & Hall): academic but comprehensive on adversarial ML fundamentals

items.title: Best AI Tools for Beginners to Try in 2026: The Amazing List
items.summary: Trying to pick the right software used to mean comparing a handful of options and reading a few reviews. In 2026, it means wading through hundreds of new launches every single month, each one claiming to be the smartest, fastest, or most powerful option available. If that feels overwhelming, you are not alone, and this roundup of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 was put together specifically to cut through that noise, using plain language instead of technical marketing terms. Instead of listing every tool under the sun, this guide focuses on options that are genuinely approachable for someone who has never touched an AI product before. No technical background is assumed, and every recommendation here comes with a clear explanation of what it actually does, who it is best suited for, and why it earned a place among the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. Why Beginners Need a Different Kind of List Most “best AI tools” articles are written for marketers, developers, or power users who already understand prompts, APIs, and workflows. That approach leaves genuine beginners feeling lost before they even open the first app. A proper list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 should instead prioritize simplicity, a gentle learning curve, and tools that deliver value within the first five minutes of use. Before jumping into the list, it helps to understand what “beginner-friendly” actually means in this context. It means a clean interface without a wall of settings, a free tier generous enough to actually learn on, and clear guidance inside the tool itself rather than a confusing blank text box. Every tool featured in this best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 guide was chosen with those exact criteria in mind. How to Choose the Right AI Tool as a Beginner Picking your first tool does not need to be complicated if you start by asking yourself one simple question: what task do I actually want help with? Someone who wants help writing emails has very different needs from someone who wants to organize research notes or generate images for a small business. A second useful filter is cost. Nearly every entry in this best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 list offers a usable free plan, so you can test several options before committing any money. A third filter is platform availability. Some tools work only through a web browser, while others offer mobile apps, browser extensions, or both, which matters if you plan to use them on the go. Finally, pay attention to how the tool explains itself. A beginner-friendly product usually includes example prompts, short onboarding tutorials, or suggested starting points instead of dropping you into an empty screen and hoping for the best. Where to Use These Tools: Web, App, or Browser Extension Another practical factor beginners often overlook is where a tool actually lives. Some of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 work primarily through a web browser, which is fine if you mostly work at a desk, but less convenient if you want quick help on your phone throughout the day. Others offer dedicated mobile apps, letting you draft a message or check a fact while standing in line at the grocery store. A smaller number integrate directly as browser extensions, quietly working in the background inside whatever website or document you already have open. Thinking about your daily routine before choosing between these formats will help you pick from the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 based on how you actually work, not just which tool has the flashiest homepage. The Best AI Tools for Beginners to Try in 2026 ChatGPT remains one of the easiest entry points for anyone exploring the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. Its simple chat interface handles everyday writing, brainstorming, summarizing, and even basic problem-solving without requiring any setup. The free tier is generous enough for regular personal use, and its widespread popularity means there are countless beginner tutorials available if you get stuck. Google Gemini is another strong pick, particularly for anyone already living inside the Google ecosystem. Because it connects directly to your Gmail, Docs, and Calendar, it can summarize long email threads, draft documents, and even handle voice conversations through Gemini Live. This deep integration makes it one of the more practical options in any list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026, since it fits naturally into tasks you are already doing. Perplexity AI takes a different approach by functioning as an intelligent research assistant rather than a general chatbot. When you ask it a question, it searches the web in real time and shows you the exact sources behind its answer, which builds trust and makes fact-checking simple. For beginners who want to use AI specifically for research or learning, Perplexity is consistently recommended across nearly every roundup of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. Grammarly deserves a spot on this list even though many people do not think of it as an “AI tool” in the traditional sense. It works quietly inside your browser or documents, correcting grammar, improving clarity, and adjusting tone as you type. Because it requires zero extra effort to learn, it is often the very first AI-powered tool a complete beginner ever uses without realizing it. NotebookLM is a slightly different kind of tool built around your own material rather than the open internet. You upload your notes, PDFs, or documents, and it answers questions strictly based on what you provided, making it excellent for students or anyone studying a specific topic. This focus on personal source material makes it a standout entry among the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 for anyone in an academic or research-heavy role. Canva’s AI features round out this list nicely for beginners interested in visual content rather than text. Simple prompts can generate social media graphics, presentation slides, or marketing images without any design experience required. For small business owners or content creators just starting out, this is often the most immediately useful tool on any list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. Comparing These Tools at a Glance Each of these tools solves a slightly different problem, so thinking about them by use case rather than by brand name will help you choose faster. If your main goal is everyday writing and brainstorming, ChatGPT is the most flexible starting point. If you live inside Google’s apps daily, Gemini will feel more natural because it already has access to your existing files and calendar. For research-heavy tasks where accuracy and sources matter, Perplexity is the strongest choice among the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026, since it shows its work instead of just giving you an answer. Grammarly is best treated as a background helper you barely notice rather than a tool you actively open and use. NotebookLM shines specifically when you already have your own documents and want answers grounded only in that material. Canva is the obvious pick the moment your task involves anything visual rather than purely text-based. Common Mistakes Beginners Make When Starting Out One frequent mistake is trying to learn five tools at once instead of picking one and actually using it for a week. Spreading your attention too thin makes it hard to build real comfort with any single option. A better approach with any list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 is to choose one tool that matches your most common task, use it daily for a short period, and only then explore a second option. Another common mistake is expecting perfect results on the very first try. These tools respond better to clear, specific instructions than vague ones, so beginners often need a few attempts before they get comfortable phrasing requests well. Writing “help me with my email” produces a far weaker result than writing “write a polite follow-up email to a client who has not responded in two weeks.” A third mistake is ignoring privacy settings entirely. Many of these tools offer options to control whether your conversations are used for training or saved long term. Reviewing these settings early, rather than after the fact, is a habit every beginner exploring the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 should build from day one. Who Should Wait Before Trying These Tools Not everyone needs to jump in immediately, and that is perfectly fine. If you are dealing with highly sensitive work involving confidential client data, medical records, or legal documents, it is worth waiting until you fully understand a tool’s privacy policy before using it for that specific purpose, even if it appears elsewhere on a list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. There is no rush, and starting with lower-stakes, personal tasks first is always the safer path. Free vs Paid Plans: What Beginners Should Know Every tool mentioned in this best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 guide offers a workable free plan, which means you genuinely do not need to spend money to get started. Free plans typically include usage limits, such as a maximum number of messages per day or slightly slower response times during busy periods, but they are more than enough for learning and light personal use. Paid plans generally unlock higher usage limits, access to more advanced underlying models, and extra features like larger file uploads or priority processing. As a beginner, there is rarely a good reason to upgrade immediately. A smarter approach is to use the free tier for at least a few weeks, notice exactly where you hit limitations, and only then decide whether a paid plan solves a real problem you have actually experienced firsthand. Tips for Getting More Value From Any AI Tool A few small habits make a noticeable difference no matter which option you pick from this list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026. Be specific in your requests, since detailed instructions almost always produce more useful results than short, vague ones. Save prompts that worked well so you can reuse and tweak them later instead of rewriting from scratch every time. It also helps to treat these tools as a starting draft rather than a finished product. Even the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 can make mistakes, misunderstand context, or produce generic output, so reviewing and editing the result yourself will always give you a better final version than accepting the first response blindly. How These Tools Connect to AI Agents If you have already read about how AI agents work, you will notice that some of the tools in this best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 list are beginning to blur that line. Several chat platforms now offer agent-like modes that can complete multi-step tasks rather than answering a single question. Trying these features is a natural next step once you feel comfortable with basic chat-based usage. For a deeper explanation of how that technology works under the hood, our guide on AI agents for beginners explained breaks the concept down without any technical jargon. According to PCMag’s tested picks for AI chatbots , overall usefulness for everyday users depends less on raw technical power and more on ease of use and reliability, which lines up closely with the beginner-first philosophy behind this entire list. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best AI tool for a complete beginner? ChatGPT is generally the easiest starting point because of its simple interface, generous free tier, and huge number of beginner tutorials available online. Are these AI tools really free to use? Yes, every tool mentioned offers a genuinely usable free plan, though most also offer optional paid upgrades for heavier or more advanced use. Do I need any technical skills to use these tools? No. Every tool on this list of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 was chosen specifically because it requires no coding or technical background to get started. Which AI tool is best for students? NotebookLM is particularly well suited for students because it answers questions based strictly on uploaded notes, textbooks, or PDFs rather than the open internet. Can I use more than one AI tool at the same time? Yes, many people eventually use two or three tools for different purposes, such as one for writing and another for research, though beginners should start with just one. Is it safe to share personal information with these tools? You should always review each tool’s privacy settings and avoid sharing highly sensitive personal or financial details, since policies on data retention vary between providers. How do I know when I am ready to try more advanced AI tools? Once you feel confident using a beginner tool daily without confusion, and you find yourself wanting features it does not offer, that is usually a good sign you are ready to explore more advanced options. Do these tools work well outside English-speaking countries? Most of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 support multiple languages reasonably well, though quality can vary, so it is worth testing a tool in your preferred language before relying on it heavily. What if a tool on this list gets discontinued or changes its pricing? The AI space moves quickly, so features and pricing can shift. If that happens, the good news is that the underlying skills you build, like writing clear prompts, transfer easily to whichever best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 you switch to next. Conclusion Choosing your first AI tool does not need to be stressful, even with so many new options appearing every month. This guide to the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 was built to simplify that decision by focusing only on tools that are genuinely approachable, well-supported by free plans, and useful from the very first session. Start with the one tool that matches your biggest daily task, spend real time with it, and expand from there once you feel confident, since consistency matters far more than trying every option from this best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 list at once. The beginners who make the most progress are rarely the ones chasing every new release. They are the ones who pick a solid starting point from a list like this one and actually build a habit around it. If you found this roundup of the best AI tools for beginners to try in 2026 helpful, bookmark it and revisit it whenever you are ready to add a new tool to your toolkit, since new beginner-friendly options are added throughout the year. items.title: Context Engineering Inside the Harness: 4 Mechanisms That Beat Context Overflow and Goal Loss on Long-Horizon Tasks
items.summary: An agent, in its simplest form, is an LLM calling tools in a loop. That loop works for short jobs. Give it a task that runs for an hour and 200 tool calls, and it breaks in 2 predictable ways. The AWS Samples design guide for autonomous cloud coding agents names them directly: shallow agents suffer from context overflow, get distracted (goal loss), and do not maintain state over long periods. The layer that fixes this is not the model. It is the harness, which AWS describes as managing everything but the model. This article opens up that layer. Compaction, memory strategy, context budgeting, and todo-state are the machinery that turns a shallow loop into a deep agent. We look at how LangChain Deep Agents , Claude Code , Manus , OpenAI Codex , and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore implement each one, with the actual thresholds they ship. Why a bigger window does not fix it The obvious fix is a larger context window. The evidence says it helps less than expected. Chroma’s Context Rot report evaluated 18 LLMs, including GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and Qwen3, and found that performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows, even on simple retrieval tasks. Anthropic’s context engineering guide explains the mechanism: attention creates n² pairwise relationships for n tokens, so every added token depletes a finite “attention budget.” Context is a resource with diminishing returns, not a bucket. For an agent loop, this is worse than it sounds. Manus reports that a typical task needs around 50 tool calls, and that the input-to-output token ratio runs near 100:1. Each observation lands in context and stays there. The original instruction drifts toward the middle of the window, which is exactly where recall degrades. Goal loss is not only a model bug. It is the expected outcome of an unmanaged context on a long enough task. Mechanism 1: Context budgeting and offloading The first job of a harness is deciding what never enters the window at all. Deep Agents ships 2 offloading rules with hard numbers. When a tool response exceeds 20,000 tokens, it is written to the filesystem and replaced with a file path plus a preview of the first 10 lines. When session context crosses 85% of the model’s window, older write and edit tool calls, whose full file contents already live on disk, are truncated to a pointer. Only after offloading runs out of room does the harness fall back to summarization. Claude Code applies the same budgeting to what loads before the first prompt. Auto memory is capped at the first 200 lines or 25KB. MCP tool schemas stay deferred by default, with only tool names listed, and full schemas load on demand via tool search. After compaction, any re-read file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference rather than content. The context window simulation in the Claude Code docs makes the payoff concrete: a research subagent reads 6,100 tokens of files and returns a 420-token result to the parent. That subagent pattern is budgeting at the architecture level. Anthropic’s guide notes that each subagent may burn tens of thousands of tokens exploring, but returns a distilled summary, often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. The AWS AgentCore walkthrough builds exactly this: a coordinator spawns 3 browser subagents in parallel, each in its own MicroVM, and an analyst subagent receives only their structured findings. AWS reports a 4 to 6 minute expected runtime, and notes that sequential processing would take up to 3x longer. Mechanism 2: Compaction When offloading is not enough, the harness summarizes. Compaction is the practice of taking a conversation nearing the window limit, summarizing it, and reinitiating a new context with the summary. It is also where goal loss most often happens, because a lossy summary can drop the one constraint that mattered. The implementations differ in what they promise to keep. Claude Code’s compaction prompt preserves architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs. Right after compaction it re-reads up to 5 of the files modified most recently, reloads the rules matching those files, and re-injects invoked skill bodies, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 total. The docs are explicit that detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost, which is why persistent rules belong in the project-root CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected from disk. Users can steer the pass with /compact focus on the auth bug fix or move the trigger point with /autocompact . Deep Agents made goal preservation a structural feature. Its summary is a structured document with dedicated fields for session intent, artifacts created, and next steps. The LangChain team added those fields after forced-summarization experiments showed the change improved performance. The full original transcript is also written to the filesystem, so a fact that was summarized away can be recovered by read_file later. Compaction has moved into the API layer too. OpenAI’s Responses API offers server-side compaction via context_management with a compact_threshold , plus a standalone /responses/compact endpoint that returns a compacted context window containing an opaque encrypted compaction item; OpenAI instructs developers to pass that returned window unchanged into the next call. OpenAI says Codex relies on this mechanism to sustain long-running coding tasks. The Claude Developer Platform exposes a compact_20260112 context-management edit with custom instructions and a pause_after_compaction option for inserting content before the model continues. When you write custom instructions there, they replace the default prompt entirely, so a compaction prompt is a real engineering artifact, not a setting. Mechanism 3: Todo-state and recitation Compaction protects the goal at the moment of summarization. Todo-state protects it on every turn in between. Manus described the trick plainly: its agent creates a todo.md and rewrites it step by step, checking items off. Rewriting the list recites the objectives into the end of the context, pushing the global plan into the model’s recent attention span and reducing “lost in the middle” drift. No architecture change is required. It is natural language used to bias the model’s own attention. The evidence on todo-state is not one-sided. Deep Agents shipped a write_todos tool by default until v0.7 in July 2026 , when LangChain made TodoListMiddleware opt-in after its evals across 3 task categories showed slightly better reward and lower cost with todos disabled. LangChain still recommends turning it back on for long multi-step tasks, less capable models, and UIs that show progress. Claude Code keeps a todo list and re-injects the plan written in plan mode from disk after compaction. Anthropic’s guide calls the general pattern structured note-taking: the agent writes a NOTES.md or TODO file outside the window and reloads it. Its Claude Plays Pokémon example maintained tallies across thousands of game steps, then read its own notes after each context reset and resumed multi-hour sequences. The pattern behind all of these is that the goal exists as a mutable artifact, not only as a message in history. Messages age and get summarized. A file that is rewritten every few turns is always recent, always short, and survives any reset. Whether that is worth its per-turn token cost depends on the model and the task length, which is exactly what the Deep Agents evals measured. Mechanism 4: Memory strategy across sessions The last piece is what persists after the task ends. Claude Code re-injects the project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory from disk after every compaction. AgentCore Memory stores events and runs configured extraction strategies in the background, so a coordinator can call a recall tool on the next run instead of re-researching. AWS warns that without at least 1 extraction strategy configured, raw events are stored but nothing is extracted for retrieval. Anthropic’s file-based memory tool serves the same purpose on the Claude platform. The limitation is that persistent context is not free. The ETH Zurich study we covered in February found that repository context files like AGENTS.md do not generally improve task success while raising inference cost: LLM-generated files increased cost by 20% and 23% on the 2 benchmarks, and developer-committed files by up to 19%. Memory that reloads every session is a standing tax on the attention budget. The Claude Code docs give the matching advice: keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move reference material into skills or path-scoped rules that load only when needed. Interactive explainer: watch a 200K window fill up The simulator below runs a 60-step migration task through a 200K token window. Toggle the 4 mechanisms, set the compaction trigger, and press Run. With everything off, the window overflows before the task is half done. With offloading, compaction, todo recitation, and subagent delegation on, the same task finishes with the goal still in recent attention. Token counts are illustrative; the thresholds match Deep Agents defaults. & Testing whether the harness actually holds the goal Context management is only useful if the agent can still finish the task and recover details it no longer sees. LangChain maintains targeted evals for exactly this: tests that trigger summarization mid-task and check whether the agent continues toward its objective, and needle-in-a-haystack cases where a fact is summarized away and must be recovered through filesystem search. To generate enough events to compare prompt variants, the team triggers summarization at 10 to 20% of the window instead of the 85% default, and used a 25% trigger with Claude Sonnet 4.5 on terminal-bench-2 to study the effect. The failure to watch for, in LangChain’s view, is goal drift: an agent that asks for clarification right after a summary, or wrongly declares the task complete. AgentCore Evaluations ships a goal success rate evaluator that can score the same traces. If you run a harness and have not forced a compaction in a test, you do not yet know what your summary prompt drops. Key Takeaways Shallow agents fail from context overflow and goal loss; the harness, not the model, is where the fix lives. Budget first: Deep Agents offloads tool results over 20,000 tokens and evicts old edits at 85% of the window. Compaction must name what it keeps; Deep Agents adds session intent and next steps fields, Claude Code re-reads 5 recent files. Todo recitation keeps the goal at the end of context, but Deep Agents v0.7 evals show it is not a free win. Persistent memory costs attention: ETH Zurich measured 20 to 23% higher inference cost from LLM-generated context files. The post Context Engineering Inside the Harness: 4 Mechanisms That Beat Context Overflow and Goal Loss on Long-Horizon Tasks appeared first on MarkTechPost .
items.summary_html:
An agent, in its simplest form, is an LLM calling tools in a loop. That loop works for short jobs. Give it a task that runs for an hour and 200 tool calls, and it breaks in 2 predictable ways. The AWS Samples design guide for autonomous cloud coding agents names them directly: shallow agents suffer from context overflow, get distracted (goal loss), and do not maintain state over long periods. The layer that fixes this is not the model. It is the harness, which AWS describes as managing everything but the model.

This article opens up that layer. Compaction, memory strategy, context budgeting, and todo-state are the machinery that turns a shallow loop into a deep agent. We look at how LangChain Deep Agents, Claude Code, Manus, OpenAI Codex, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore implement each one, with the actual thresholds they ship.

Why a bigger window does not fix it

The obvious fix is a larger context window. The evidence says it helps less than expected. Chroma’s Context Rot report evaluated 18 LLMs, including GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and Qwen3, and found that performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows, even on simple retrieval tasks. Anthropic’s context engineering guide explains the mechanism: attention creates n² pairwise relationships for n tokens, so every added token depletes a finite “attention budget.” Context is a resource with diminishing returns, not a bucket.

For an agent loop, this is worse than it sounds. Manus reports that a typical task needs around 50 tool calls, and that the input-to-output token ratio runs near 100:1. Each observation lands in context and stays there. The original instruction drifts toward the middle of the window, which is exactly where recall degrades. Goal loss is not only a model bug. It is the expected outcome of an unmanaged context on a long enough task.

Mechanism 1: Context budgeting and offloading

The first job of a harness is deciding what never enters the window at all. Deep Agents ships 2 offloading rules with hard numbers. When a tool response exceeds 20,000 tokens, it is written to the filesystem and replaced with a file path plus a preview of the first 10 lines. When session context crosses 85% of the model’s window, older write and edit tool calls, whose full file contents already live on disk, are truncated to a pointer. Only after offloading runs out of room does the harness fall back to summarization.

Claude Code applies the same budgeting to what loads before the first prompt. Auto memory is capped at the first 200 lines or 25KB. MCP tool schemas stay deferred by default, with only tool names listed, and full schemas load on demand via tool search. After compaction, any re-read file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference rather than content. The context window simulation in the Claude Code docs makes the payoff concrete: a research subagent reads 6,100 tokens of files and returns a 420-token result to the parent.

That subagent pattern is budgeting at the architecture level. Anthropic’s guide notes that each subagent may burn tens of thousands of tokens exploring, but returns a distilled summary, often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. The AWS AgentCore walkthrough builds exactly this: a coordinator spawns 3 browser subagents in parallel, each in its own MicroVM, and an analyst subagent receives only their structured findings. AWS reports a 4 to 6 minute expected runtime, and notes that sequential processing would take up to 3x longer.

Mechanism 2: Compaction

When offloading is not enough, the harness summarizes. Compaction is the practice of taking a conversation nearing the window limit, summarizing it, and reinitiating a new context with the summary. It is also where goal loss most often happens, because a lossy summary can drop the one constraint that mattered.

The implementations differ in what they promise to keep. Claude Code’s compaction prompt preserves architectural decisions, unresolved bugs, and implementation details while discarding redundant tool outputs. Right after compaction it re-reads up to 5 of the files modified most recently, reloads the rules matching those files, and re-injects invoked skill bodies, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 total. The docs are explicit that detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost, which is why persistent rules belong in the project-root CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected from disk. Users can steer the pass with /compact focus on the auth bug fix or move the trigger point with /autocompact.

Deep Agents made goal preservation a structural feature. Its summary is a structured document with dedicated fields for session intent, artifacts created, and next steps. The LangChain team added those fields after forced-summarization experiments showed the change improved performance. The full original transcript is also written to the filesystem, so a fact that was summarized away can be recovered by read_file later.

Compaction has moved into the API layer too. OpenAI’s Responses API offers server-side compaction via context_management with a compact_threshold, plus a standalone /responses/compact endpoint that returns a compacted context window containing an opaque encrypted compaction item; OpenAI instructs developers to pass that returned window unchanged into the next call. OpenAI says Codex relies on this mechanism to sustain long-running coding tasks. The Claude Developer Platform exposes a compact_20260112 context-management edit with custom instructions and a pause_after_compaction option for inserting content before the model continues. When you write custom instructions there, they replace the default prompt entirely, so a compaction prompt is a real engineering artifact, not a setting.

Mechanism 3: Todo-state and recitation

Compaction protects the goal at the moment of summarization. Todo-state protects it on every turn in between. Manus described the trick plainly: its agent creates a todo.md and rewrites it step by step, checking items off. Rewriting the list recites the objectives into the end of the context, pushing the global plan into the model’s recent attention span and reducing “lost in the middle” drift. No architecture change is required. It is natural language used to bias the model’s own attention.

The evidence on todo-state is not one-sided. Deep Agents shipped a write_todos tool by default until v0.7 in July 2026, when LangChain made TodoListMiddleware opt-in after its evals across 3 task categories showed slightly better reward and lower cost with todos disabled. LangChain still recommends turning it back on for long multi-step tasks, less capable models, and UIs that show progress. Claude Code keeps a todo list and re-injects the plan written in plan mode from disk after compaction. Anthropic’s guide calls the general pattern structured note-taking: the agent writes a NOTES.md or TODO file outside the window and reloads it. Its Claude Plays Pokémon example maintained tallies across thousands of game steps, then read its own notes after each context reset and resumed multi-hour sequences.

The pattern behind all of these is that the goal exists as a mutable artifact, not only as a message in history. Messages age and get summarized. A file that is rewritten every few turns is always recent, always short, and survives any reset. Whether that is worth its per-turn token cost depends on the model and the task length, which is exactly what the Deep Agents evals measured.

Mechanism 4: Memory strategy across sessions

The last piece is what persists after the task ends. Claude Code re-injects the project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory from disk after every compaction. AgentCore Memory stores events and runs configured extraction strategies in the background, so a coordinator can call a recall tool on the next run instead of re-researching. AWS warns that without at least 1 extraction strategy configured, raw events are stored but nothing is extracted for retrieval. Anthropic’s file-based memory tool serves the same purpose on the Claude platform.

The limitation is that persistent context is not free. The ETH Zurich study we covered in February found that repository context files like AGENTS.md do not generally improve task success while raising inference cost: LLM-generated files increased cost by 20% and 23% on the 2 benchmarks, and developer-committed files by up to 19%. Memory that reloads every session is a standing tax on the attention budget. The Claude Code docs give the matching advice: keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and move reference material into skills or path-scoped rules that load only when needed.

Interactive explainer: watch a 200K window fill up

The simulator below runs a 60-step migration task through a 200K token window. Toggle the 4 mechanisms, set the compaction trigger, and press Run. With everything off, the window overflows before the task is half done. With offloading, compaction, todo recitation, and subagent delegation on, the same task finishes with the goal still in recent attention. Token counts are illustrative; the thresholds match Deep Agents defaults.

&

Testing whether the harness actually holds the goal

Context management is only useful if the agent can still finish the task and recover details it no longer sees. LangChain maintains targeted evals for exactly this: tests that trigger summarization mid-task and check whether the agent continues toward its objective, and needle-in-a-haystack cases where a fact is summarized away and must be recovered through filesystem search. To generate enough events to compare prompt variants, the team triggers summarization at 10 to 20% of the window instead of the 85% default, and used a 25% trigger with Claude Sonnet 4.5 on terminal-bench-2 to study the effect.

The failure to watch for, in LangChain’s view, is goal drift: an agent that asks for clarification right after a summary, or wrongly declares the task complete. AgentCore Evaluations ships a goal success rate evaluator that can score the same traces. If you run a harness and have not forced a compaction in a test, you do not yet know what your summary prompt drops.

Key Takeaways
  • Shallow agents fail from context overflow and goal loss; the harness, not the model, is where the fix lives.
  • Budget first: Deep Agents offloads tool results over 20,000 tokens and evicts old edits at 85% of the window.
  • Compaction must name what it keeps; Deep Agents adds session intent and next steps fields, Claude Code re-reads 5 recent files.
  • Todo recitation keeps the goal at the end of context, but Deep Agents v0.7 evals show it is not a free win.
  • Persistent memory costs attention: ETH Zurich measured 20 to 23% higher inference cost from LLM-generated context files.

items.title: A Telegram job alert bot in 60 lines of Python, on live ATS data
items.summary_html:
Job boards go stale fast. By the time a weekly digest reaches you, the interesting roles have been open
for a month. So let's build the smallest thing that fixes that: a Telegram bot that wakes up, asks one
API for everything posted in the last seven days, and sends you the new ones.

Sixty lines, no framework, no database.

The data

We'll read HiringIndex — job postings taken from
the catalogue APIs that applicant tracking systems publish, so every row carries the employer's own
apply link rather than an aggregator's redirect.

One call tells you what a slice looks like before you write any code. Two slices, both measured live at
2026-09-13 04:47–04:50 UTC:

All remote, last 7 days Python roles, remote, last 7 days Postings 10,860 9 Companies 2,227 8 Median days open 4 — Posted in the last 7 days 100% 100%

The second column is the filter the bot below actually uses, and it is deliberately narrow — nine
postings is a morning's worth of reading, not a firehose. Widen it by dropping job_titles and you
are back to the first column.

Salaries do not come from search at all: they come from /jobs/insights, per currency, and each
percentile says how many disclosures it rests on — for the wide slice, 744 USD postings give p25
115,000–150,000, p50 155,650–200,000, p75 199,000–260,000. Percentiles appear only where at least
30 salaries are disclosed, so a number you get is computed from real bands.

The bot 
import os
import time

import requests

API = "https://hiringindex.p.rapidapi.com/jobs/search"
HEADERS = {
    "X-RapidAPI-Key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"],
    "X-RapidAPI-Host": "hiringindex.p.rapidapi.com",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}
TELEGRAM = f"https://api.telegram.org/bot{os.environ['TG_BOT_TOKEN']}/sendMessage"
CHAT_ID = os.environ["TG_CHAT_ID"]

FILTER = {
    "job_titles": ["Python Developer"],
    "remote_flag": ["true"],
    "days_ago": 7,
    "limit": 20,
}


def fetch(page=1):
    r = requests.post(API, headers=HEADERS, json=FILTER | {"page": page}, timeout=60)
    if r.status_code == 503:                     # capacity, not an error on your side
        time.sleep(float(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 5)))
        return fetch(page)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def line(job):
    bits = [job.get("country_code"), job.get("employment_type"), job.get("seniority")]
    tail = " · ".join(b for b in bits if b)
    return (f"{job['title']}\n{job.get('company_name') or job.get('handle')}"
            f"{' · ' + tail if tail else ''}\nposted {job.get('posted_at')}\n"
            f"{job.get('apply_url') or job.get('posting_url')}")


def send(text):
    requests.post(TELEGRAM, json={"chat_id": CHAT_ID, "text": text,
                                  "parse_mode": "HTML", "disable_web_page_preview": True}, timeout=30)


def main():
    seen = set(open("seen.txt").read().split()) if os.path.exists("seen.txt") else set()
    data = fetch()
    fresh = [j for j in data["jobs"] if j["_id"] not in seen]
    for job in fresh:
        send(line(job))
        seen.add(job["_id"])
    with open("seen.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(seen))
    print(f"{len(fresh)} new of {data['total_count']} matching")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it from cron every morning. seen.txt is the whole state: a posting is sent once and never again.

Three things worth knowing before you build on it

days_ago filters by the employer's publication date, not by when the index saw the row. That is
why the median above is four days and not four hours — the filter is about the job, not about our
crawler.

Rows are not postings. A role advertised in three cities is three rows in search, one posting in
the aggregate. If you count anything, count with /jobs/insights, which deduplicates; total_count
on search is rows.

Errors arrive as one envelope. Branch on error, never on the message text:

{"error": "invalid_request", "message": "days_ago: expected an integer", "meta": {"request_id": "..."}}

An unknown filter key is rejected with 422 and the message names the valid keys, so a typo never
returns a silently wrong slice. An empty jobs array with total_count: 0 is a normal 200 — no
matches is not an error.

Making it yours

Swap the filter and the bot changes job:

  • {"keywords": ["kubernetes"], "days_ago": 3} — a stack watch
  • {"handles": ["walmart:wd504:WalmartExternal"]} — one employer's careers page, by ATS board handle
  • {"cities": ["Berlin"], "seniority": ["senior"], "salary": {"min": 80000}} — a narrow local search

Send the same filter to /jobs/insights instead of /jobs/search and you get the market around your
search — how many companies are hiring for it, where they are, and what they pay — in one request.

The free plan is 200 postings and 5 insights calls a month, no card:
get a key.

Written with an AI assistant; every number and code snippet was run against the live HiringIndex API by the team before publishing.

items.title: Record why an approach was rejected—and when to revisit it
items.summary:
Disclosure: I maintain Selvedge, an open-source decision-history tool. This article was prepared with AI assistance from Grok and Codex. The example below is hypothetical and uses plain Markdown; it does not require a particular product. A repository can show what the code does while leaving out why an apparently reasonable alternative was rejected. A later coding session then has the implementation but lacks the reason behind it. A useful decision record should help the next person answer two questions: why did we say no, and what evidence would justify revisiting that decision? Here is a small workflow you can use with Markdown files in a repository. Record the constraint behind the rejection Suppose src/cache.py::load_profile reads profiles from a shared database. You consider process-local caching, but one worker could keep serving an old profile after another worker updates it. For this example, that would violate the application's consistency requirement. Save the reasoning in a file such as docs/decisions/cache-001.md : # CACHE-001: Defer process-local profile caching Status: Rejected
Affected code: src/cache.py::load_profile
Approach considered: Cache profiles separately in each worker.

Constraint:
After an update completes, subsequent reads across workers must
observe the updated profile.

Reason for rejection:
A worker's cached profile can remain outdated after another
worker updates the database. We have no shared invalidation
mechanism that satisfies the constraint.

Current decision:
Keep the database read.

Revisit when:
A proposed invalidation design has evidence that it satisfies
the consistency requirement, including tests across workers. The constraint matters more than a bare instruction such as “do not cache profiles.” It lets someone assess the reasoning instead of inheriting an unexplained rule. Also distinguish an approach that was considered and declined from one that was implemented and rolled back. The latter can include a reproducer, failed test, or incident reference. Do not imply that an untried idea failed in production. Find the record before changing the code A file has little value if nobody reads it. Keep a short decision index, and give records concrete code paths or subsystem names that people can search. For this example: rg -n 'load_profile|profile caching' docs/decisions Before editing, read the matched record and inspect the current code. Check whether the constraint still applies, whether the implementation has changed, and whether there are later records that amend the decision. If you work with a coding agent, put this retrieval step in the task instructions. Check the result during review: can the agent identify the relevant record and explain its applicability? Having an instruction file does not guarantee that every tool or agent will follow it. Separate a review trigger from a new decision Now suppose a shared invalidation design has been implemented. That is a reason to review the rejection, not automatic proof that caching is safe. The review should examine the requirement and the evidence. For the hypothetical cache, useful cases include an update in one worker followed by a read in another, delayed invalidation, and a worker that misses an invalidation message. Passing a few tests does not establish every property of a distributed system, so state the limits of the evidence. Record the review in a linked file: # CACHE-002: Reopen the profile-caching proposal Reviews: CACHE-001 (cache-001.md)
Status: Reopened for evaluation

What changed:
A shared invalidation design is now available for review.

Evidence to assess:
The design, multi-worker tests, and failure behavior when
invalidation is delayed or missed.

Decision:
Reconsider the proposal. Caching is not yet approved. Add a link from the first record to the review while preserving the original rationale. If the proposal is later accepted, record that decision and its supporting evidence separately. The same mechanism works when the first rejection was simply wrong. Say which premise was mistaken and why. An accurately preserved record can still contain an incorrect judgment. Deliver the qualification with the advice When a decision is summarized for a later session, include its review state. “Caching was rejected” loses important context if a linked review has reopened the proposal. A date or condition on a record only helps when someone checks it. If a condition cannot be evaluated, carry that uncertainty into the summary. Keep “needs review,” “reopened,” and “accepted” distinct. For the next code review, try one small check: identify an earlier rejected approach, find its reason, and explain whether that reason still applies. That gives the record a concrete job in the development workflow.
